title: Why Cats Hide Pain — And the Signs That Give Them Away
excerpt: A cat in pain rarely cries. It gets quiet, and quiet is easy to miss.
body: *A dog in pain tells you. A cat in pain goes still, sleeps in a new place, and waits. Here is how to read the difference.*

![A cat watching from the shadows](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1478098711619-5ab0b478d6e6?auto=format&fit=crop&w=1200&q=80)
*Stillness is the most under-read symptom in cats.*
## The instinct behind the silence

Cats are both predator and prey. In the wild, an animal that limps loudly, vocalises and draws attention is the one that gets picked off. Domestic cats kept that wiring. Concealing weakness is not stoicism and it is not your cat being brave — it is an old survival reflex that has outlived its usefulness in a living room.

The practical consequence is uncomfortable: **by the time a cat looks obviously unwell, it has usually been unwell for a while.** Owners routinely report that a cat diagnosed with advanced dental disease or arthritis "was completely fine last week." It almost never was.
> Cats do not have a low pain threshold. They have a high tolerance for *showing* it.
## What actually changes first
Pain in cats shows up as **subtraction**, not addition. You are looking for things that stopped, not things that started.
### Movement

- Jumping onto the counter in two hops instead of one
- Choosing the sofa over the windowsill it always used
- Hesitating at the top of the stairs before going down
- Sleeping on the floor when it always slept up high
Height loss is the single most useful arthritis signal in cats, and roughly **90% of cats over twelve have arthritic changes on X-ray**. Very few of them limp. They just stop going up.
### Grooming
A cat's coat is a health report you can read for free.

| What you see | What it often means |
|---|---|
| Dull, clumped or greasy coat | Grooming has stopped — pain, obesity or illness |
| Dandruff along the lower back | Can't twist to reach it any more |
| One patch groomed bald | Focal pain underneath, or stress |
| Matting behind the shoulders | Reduced spinal flexibility |
### The litter tray

- Going *next to* the tray rather than in it
- Straining, or many small visits
- Crying in the tray

Litter tray changes get treated as behavioural problems and punished. In an adult cat they are a medical symptom until a vet proves otherwise. **Straining with little output in a male cat is an emergency** — a urinary blockage can kill in under 48 hours.
### Appetite and the jaw

Dental pain is common and almost invisible. Watch for chewing on one side, dropping food, approaching the bowl and walking away, or a sudden preference for wet food over kibble. That last one is a cat telling you biting hurts.
## Reading the face
Researchers at the Université de Montréal validated the **Feline Grimace Scale**, which scores five facial features. It works, and you can use a simplified version at home.

1. **Ears** — rotating outward and flattening apart
2. **Eyes** — narrowing or squinting when not sleepy
3. **Muzzle** — tightening from rounded to elliptical
4. **Whiskers** — pushed forward and straightened rather than relaxed
5. **Head** — carried level with or below the shoulders
A comfortable cat has a soft, round face with whiskers hanging loose to the side. Tension pulls everything forward and flat.

![A relaxed, loafing cat](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1519052537078-e6302a4968d4?auto=format&fit=crop&w=1200&q=80)
*The loaf with paws tucked and a soft face is a comfortable cat. The same posture with a tight muzzle and forward whiskers is not.*
## The purring trap

Purring means "I need something to change," not "I am happy." Cats purr while giving birth, while injured, and in the last hours of life. A cat purring at the vet is frequently self-soothing under stress.
**Never use purring to rule pain out.** Use posture, movement and face instead.
## A weekly two-minute check
Do this on a normal evening, not when you are already worried:

- [ ] Run both hands from ears to tail base — any flinch, twitch or turn to look?
- [ ] Check the coat over the lower back and behind the shoulders for dandruff or matting
- [ ] Lift the lip and look at the gum line for redness
- [ ] Watch one jump up and one jump down
- [ ] Note where they slept — high or low?
- [ ] Weigh monthly on a kitchen scale; **a 5% loss is significant**
Write the weight down. Trends catch what a single number never will.
## When to call the vet today
Some things do not wait for the next working day.

- Straining in the tray with little or no urine, especially in males
- Open-mouth breathing, or more than 40 breaths per minute at rest
- Hiding in an unusual place and refusing to come out
- No food for 24 hours — cats can develop **hepatic lipidosis** from short fasts
- Sudden dragging or weakness of the back legs
- Crying when picked up or touched in one spot
## The short version

Cats do not exaggerate discomfort — they under-report it. Treat any *quiet* change as loudly as you would treat a limp: a lost jump, a dull coat, a skipped meal, a new sleeping spot. You are not being paranoid. You are compensating for an instinct your cat cannot switch off.
*This article is general guidance and does not replace veterinary examination. If you think your cat is in pain, book a consultation.*

title: How to Read a Cat Food Label Without Getting Fooled
excerpt: The front of the bag is marketing. The back of the bag is the product.
body: *"Natural", "premium" and "with real chicken" are legally close to meaningless. Here is what the back of the pack actually tells you.*

![A curious cat looking over the edge of a box](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1514888286974-6c03e2ca1dba?auto=format&fit=crop&w=1200&q=80)
*Everything that matters is printed in the smallest type on the bag.*
## Start at the bottom: the adequacy statement
Before ingredients, before protein, find the one sentence that says the food is **complete and balanced**. In the US it cites AAFCO; in Europe, FEDIAF.
There are two ways a food earns it, and they are not equal:

| Wording | What it means |
|---|---|
| "…formulated to meet the nutrient levels established by…" | Checked on a spreadsheet |
| "…animal feeding tests… substantiate that it provides complete nutrition" | Actually fed to cats and measured |

Feeding-trial foods are the stronger claim. Also check the **life stage**: growth, adult maintenance, or *all life stages*. An "all life stages" food is formulated for kittens, which means it is energy-dense — fine for a growing cat, easy overfeeding for a neutered eight-year-old.
> If a package has no adequacy statement at all, it is a **treat or complementary food**, not a meal. That is legal and fine, as long as you know it.
## The ingredient list, and its favourite trick
Ingredients are listed by weight **before cooking**. That single detail creates most of the confusion.
### Fresh meat is mostly water

"Fresh chicken" is around 70% water. After extrusion, most of that weight is gone. A bag listing *chicken* first can still finish with less chicken protein than one listing **chicken meal** first, because meal is already rendered and dried — roughly 300% more protein by weight than fresh.
**Chicken meal is not a downgrade.** A named meal is a concentrated protein source.
### Named beats unnamed, always

- **Good:** chicken meal, lamb meal, salmon meal, turkey liver
- **Vague:** meat meal, poultry by-product meal, animal fat, meat and animal derivatives
The problem with unnamed sources is not that they are poison — it is that the supplier can change between batches. For a cat with a food allergy, that is the whole ball game.
### Ingredient splitting
Watch for one ingredient entered several times under different names:
> Chicken, **peas**, chicken meal, **pea protein**, **pea fibre**, **pea starch**…
Individually each sits below the chicken. Added together, peas may outweigh it. Legal, common, and worth spotting.

![Bread and wheat, a stand-in for cereal fillers](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1509440159596-0249088772ff?auto=format&fit=crop&w=1200&q=80)
*Grain is not automatically bad. Grain doing the job protein should be doing is.*
## The guaranteed analysis, and the maths everyone skips
The panel gives crude protein, fat, fibre and moisture. You cannot compare a wet food to a dry food using these numbers directly, because one is 78% water and the other is 8%.
Convert both to **dry matter basis**:

```
Dry matter % = (as-fed %) / (100 - moisture %) × 100
```
Worked example:

| | Wet food | Dry food |
|---|---|---|
| Protein as printed | 10% | 32% |
| Moisture | 78% | 8% |
| **Protein, dry matter** | **45.5%** | **34.8%** |
The wet food that *looked* like a third of the protein has considerably more. This is the single most useful calculation in pet nutrition, and almost no one does it at the shelf.
### Rough targets, dry matter basis

| Nutrient | Adult cat | Kitten |
|---|---|---|
| Protein | 40%+ | 45%+ |
| Fat | 18–30% | 20–35% |
| Carbohydrate | under 20% is preferable | as low as practical |
Carbohydrate is almost never printed. Estimate it:

```
Carbs ≈ 100 - protein - fat - fibre - ash - moisture
```
If ash is missing, assume about 6–8% for a typical complete food.
## Things that must be there

- **Taurine.** Cats cannot make enough themselves. Deficiency causes irreversible blindness and dilated cardiomyopathy. Every complete cat food lists it.
- **Vitamin A, preformed.** Cats cannot convert beta-carotene the way dogs and humans can.
- **Arachidonic acid**, from animal fat. This is one of several reasons a cat cannot be safely vegan.
## Claims worth ignoring

- **"Natural"** — loosely defined, permits plenty
- **"Human-grade"** — meaningful only if the *entire* product is made in a human food facility
- **"Grain-free"** — replaces grain with potato or pea, often at similar carbohydrate levels
- **"Holistic", "premium", "gourmet"** — no legal definition whatsoever
- **"With chicken"** — in many jurisdictions can mean as little as **4%**
The picture of a salmon fillet on the front is art direction. The ingredient list is the contract.
## A 60-second shelf routine

1. Find the adequacy statement, and check the life stage
2. Read the first five ingredients — are they named animal sources?
3. Scan for splitting: the same vegetable under three names
4. Convert protein to dry matter and compare like with like
5. Estimate carbs by subtraction
6. Confirm taurine is listed
7. Only now look at the price per kilo
## The short version

A cat is an obligate carnivore that evolved eating small animals: high protein, moderate fat, very little carbohydrate, and about 70% water. Judge a label by how close it gets to that, and let the marketing on the front of the bag argue with itself.
*Ask your vet before changing the diet of a cat with kidney disease, diabetes, urinary or gastrointestinal conditions. Those cases have targets of their own.*

title: What Your Cat's Tail Is Really Saying
excerpt: The tail broadcasts mood before the ears, the eyes or the voice do.
body: *Cats are not subtle. We are just reading the wrong end.*

![A ginger cat with its tail raised in a confident hook](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1596854407944-bf87f6fdd49e?auto=format&fit=crop&w=1200&q=80)
*The upright tail with a soft hook at the tip is the clearest friendly signal a cat has.*
## Why the tail is the honest channel

A cat's face is built for hunting, not for broadcasting. Its ears and whiskers move fast and subtly. The tail, by contrast, is long, high-contrast and visible from behind and at a distance — which is exactly what social signalling needs.

Behavioural research points to something striking: **the raised, vertical tail is one of the few unambiguous friendly signals in the domestic cat's repertoire**, and it is largely absent in their solitary wild ancestor. It appears to have evolved alongside living in groups with each other and with us.
When your cat walks into the room with its tail up, it is not incidental. It is a greeting.
## The vocabulary

### Tail up, straight, tip relaxed
**Confident and sociable.** The default approach signal. A cat doing this is open to interaction.

### Tail up with a question-mark hook
**Friendly and playful.** The hook is the softened version — this is the invitation to engage.

### Tail up and quivering
**Intense greeting excitement**, usually reserved for a favourite person at the door. Worth knowing: the same quiver against a vertical surface, with a slightly crouched rear, is **urine spraying**. Context tells them apart.

### Tail held horizontal
**Neutral.** Walking, exploring, unremarkable.

### Tail low and stiff
**Wary or defensive.** Something in the environment is being evaluated.

### Tail tucked under the body
**Fear or submission.** The cat is trying to be smaller. Do not approach; let it come out.

### Tail puffed into a bottle brush
**Fear with high arousal.** Piloerection doubles apparent size. This is a startled cat, and it can escalate to defensive aggression fast. Give it space and time — the fur takes minutes to settle.

### Tail lashing hard side to side
**Agitation.** The bigger and faster the sweep, the stronger the feeling. During petting, this is the last warning before teeth.

### Tail tip twitching only
**Concentration or mild irritation.** Common at the window watching birds. Not a threat by itself.

### Tail wrapped around another cat, or around your leg
**Affiliative bonding.** A relaxed low swish while lying down is contentment, not anger.

![A tabby on the stairs with its tail extended](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1495360010541-f48722b34f7d?auto=format&fit=crop&w=1200&q=80)
*Read the tail together with the ears and the body. One signal alone is a guess.*
## The one that gets people bitten
**Petting-induced overstimulation** is the most common misread in the home. The sequence is always the same, and it always announces itself:

1. Cat settles and purrs
2. Tail tip begins to twitch
3. Skin along the back ripples
4. Ears rotate sideways or back
5. Tail begins to thump the sofa
6. Head turns toward your hand
7. Bite
Most people notice at step 6 or 7. **The signal was at step 2.** Stop at the twitch and the same cat will happily come back for more in a few minutes.
A useful habit: pet for three seconds, then pause with your hand still. If the cat leans back in, continue. If it does not, you have your answer.
## Reading the whole animal
The tail carries the volume, not the meaning. Combine it:

| Tail | Ears | Body | Reading |
|---|---|---|---|
| Up, hooked | Forward | Loose, walking to you | Come and say hello |
| Puffed | Flat sideways | Arched, sideways stance | Frightened — retreat |
| Lashing | Rotated back | Tense, still | Stop what you are doing |
| Low swish | Neutral | Lying, eyes half shut | Relaxed and content |
| Tucked | Flat back | Crouched, hiding | Very frightened or in pain |
## The slow blink

Not a tail, but the best thing you can do with this knowledge. A 2020 study at the Universities of Sussex and Portsmouth found that when humans slow-blinked at cats, the cats were **more likely to slow-blink back and more likely to approach the person's outstretched hand** — including with strangers.
The method is simple:

1. Relax your face and avoid a hard stare
2. Narrow your eyes slowly, then close them for about a second
3. Open them slowly and look slightly away
It is the closest thing we have to a cat-legible "I mean you no harm."

![A happy cat looking up](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1543852786-1cf6624b9987?auto=format&fit=crop&w=1200&q=80)
*Ears forward, whiskers loose, tail up: an unambiguously comfortable cat.*
## Tail changes that are medical, not emotional
Do not interpret these — get them checked:

- A tail suddenly carried limp or dragging, especially after a fall or a door
- Pain or crying when the tail base is touched
- Loss of tail movement together with urinary or faecal accidents
- Obsessive chasing or biting of the tail
The tail is an extension of the spine. Nerve injury at its base can affect bladder control and is urgent.
## The short version
Your cat has been narrating its mood all along, in a channel most people never learn to read. Watch the tail first, confirm with the ears, and stop when the tip starts to twitch.

title: Why Your Cat Barely Drinks — And Why It Matters
excerpt: A cat's thirst drive is broken by design. Its kidneys pay the bill.
body: *Cats evolved in deserts, hunting animals that were three-quarters water. The bowl was never part of the plan.*

![A cat drinking from a bowl](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1571131116858-2295ade82a72?auto=format&fit=crop&w=1200&q=80)
*Most cats drink less than they need, and look perfectly normal doing it.*
## The desert inheritance

The domestic cat descends from *Felis lybica*, the African wildcat, an animal that rarely met standing water. It got its fluid from prey. A mouse is roughly **70% water**, so a cat eating six or eight mice a day is effectively drinking all day long.

That left cats with two quirks we still live with. Their thirst response is weak, triggering later and less strongly than a dog's. And their kidneys are extraordinary concentrators, producing urine several times more concentrated than ours.
Both were advantages in a desert. In a kitchen with a bowl of kibble, they are liabilities.
## The kibble arithmetic

| Diet | Water in food | Water drunk | Rough daily total |
|---|---|---|---|
| Wet food only | High | Low | Adequate |
| Mixed | Moderate | Moderate | Usually adequate |
| Dry food only | About 8% | Increases, but rarely enough | Often short |
Cats on dry food do drink more. Study after study finds they do **not** drink enough more to close the gap. The shortfall is small, chronic, and invisible.
> A cat eating only dry food takes in noticeably less total water per day than the same cat on wet food. The deficit does not show as thirst. It shows as concentrated urine.
## What concentrated urine actually costs
Two problems follow, and both are common enough that most owners meet one eventually.

**Feline lower urinary tract disease.** Concentrated urine encourages crystals to form, irritates the bladder wall, and in male cats can lead to a **urethral blockage** — a genuine emergency that can kill within a day or two.

**Chronic kidney disease.** Extremely common in older cats. Hydration does not cause or cure it, but a well-hydrated kidney has an easier job, and once disease is diagnosed, water intake becomes part of the treatment.

![A cat resting quietly](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1519052537078-e6302a4968d4?auto=format&fit=crop&w=1200&q=80)
*Early dehydration looks like nothing at all. That is the whole problem.*
## Nine things that actually work
Ranked roughly by how much difference they make.

1. **Feed wet food**, even partially. Nothing else comes close. One wet meal a day changes the daily total more than any bowl trick.
2. **Add water to wet food.** A tablespoon stirred in is usually accepted without complaint.
3. **Move the bowl away from the food.** Cats instinctively avoid drinking beside a carcass. The food bowl is the carcass.
4. **Move it away from the litter tray too.** Obvious once said, frequently ignored.
5. **Use a wide, shallow bowl.** Deep narrow bowls press on the whiskers, and many cats dislike it enough to drink less.
6. **Offer several stations** in different rooms. Cats drink opportunistically as they pass.
7. **Try a fountain.** Moving water is more attractive to many cats, and safer-smelling by instinct. Not every cat cares.
8. **Change the water daily.** Cats detect staleness long before we do.
9. **Try a different material.** Some cats refuse plastic, which holds odours; ceramic, glass and steel are better.
## How to tell if a cat is dehydrated

- **Skin tent.** Lift the skin between the shoulder blades. It should fall back instantly. Slow return suggests dehydration, though it is unreliable in thin or elderly cats.
- **Gums.** They should be moist. Tacky or dry gums are a warning sign.
- **Urine clumps.** Sudden small clumps in the tray mean less urine.
**Call a vet the same day** if a cat is straining with little output, crying in the tray, or has stopped eating.
## The short version
Your cat is not being difficult. It is running desert software in a centrally heated flat. The single most effective fix is wet food; everything else is a useful nudge.
*General guidance only. Increased drinking is also an early sign of kidney disease, diabetes and hyperthyroidism — a cat that suddenly starts drinking a lot needs a vet, not a bigger bowl.*

title: The Mouth Problem Most Cats Have by Three
excerpt: Dental disease is the most common diagnosis in cats, and the least visible.
body: *By their third birthday, most cats have some degree of dental disease. Almost none of them show it.*

![Close-up of a cat with its mouth open](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1681396990341-ee6e4bd0a7bf?auto=format&fit=crop&w=1200&q=80)
*A rare clear look inside. Take it when you can get it.*
## Why it goes unnoticed

A cat with a painful mouth keeps eating. It has to. Refusing food is not an option its instincts allow, so it adapts instead: chewing on one side, swallowing kibble whole, or quietly preferring the soft food.
Owners read those adaptations as fussiness. The cat is managing pain.
## The three things that go wrong

### Gingivitis and periodontal disease
Plaque hardens into tartar within days. Tartar irritates the gum, the gum recedes, and bacteria reach the root and the bone beneath. This is the common path, and the early stage is reversible.

### Tooth resorption
The tooth structure dissolves from within, and the body replaces it with bone-like tissue. It affects a large share of adult cats, its cause is still not understood, and **it is reliably painful**. It cannot be brushed away — the treatment is extraction.

### Stomatitis
Severe, widespread inflammation of the mouth, thought to be an immune overreaction to plaque. Uncommon but debilitating. Full-mouth extraction sounds drastic and often transforms the cat.
## Signs worth acting on

| Sign | What it suggests |
|---|---|
| Bad breath | The most common early clue — not normal in a healthy cat |
| Red line along the gum | Gingivitis |
| Drooling, sometimes blood-tinged | Painful mouth |
| Chewing on one side, dropping food | Localised pain |
| Suddenly preferring wet food | Biting hurts |
| Pawing at the mouth, head shaking | Advanced discomfort |
| Yellow-brown crust on the teeth | Established tartar |
> Bad breath is the sign owners most often dismiss and vets most often act on. A healthy cat's mouth does not smell offensive.

![A relaxed cat at rest](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1518791841217-8f162f1e1131?auto=format&fit=crop&w=1200&q=80)
*Comfortable cats groom fully and eat evenly. Both change quietly when the mouth hurts.*
## What actually prevents it
**Brushing is the gold standard**, and nothing else is close. Daily is ideal, three times a week is genuinely useful, and less than weekly does very little.
To start, over a week or two:

1. Let the cat lick a little pet toothpaste off your finger. Never human toothpaste — fluoride and xylitol are toxic to cats.
2. Touch the outside of the cheek with a finger, then stop. Reward.
3. Progress to rubbing the outer surface of the canines with a fingertip.
4. Introduce a soft brush or finger brush at the same angle.
5. Brush only the **outer** surfaces. The tongue handles much of the inside.
If it becomes a fight, stop. A stressed cat and a bitten owner is a worse outcome than an unbrushed tooth.
### Second-tier options

- **Dental diets** with larger, fibrous kibble that the tooth sinks into rather than shattering
- **Products carrying a veterinary dental accreditation mark**, which means tested rather than merely claimed
- **Water additives and dental treats** — modest effects, but better than nothing for a cat that will not tolerate a brush
Ordinary dry food does **not** clean teeth. Standard kibble shatters on contact, well above the gum line where the problem lives.
## What a professional clean involves
A proper dental requires **general anaesthesia**. There is no way around it: the work goes under the gum line, and full-mouth X-rays are the only way to see resorption and root disease.
Anaesthesia-free dentistry scrapes visible tartar off the crown. It looks better and treats nothing, while giving false reassurance.
## The short version

Assume your cat has some dental disease, because the odds say it does. Smell its breath, lift its lip once a month, and ask your vet to look properly at every check-up. A cat with a comfortable mouth is a different animal.
*General guidance only. Any suspected dental pain needs veterinary examination.*

title: Caring for a Cat Over Ten
excerpt: Old age is not a disease. It is a period when several diseases become likely.
body: *"He's just slowing down because he's old" is the sentence that delays more feline diagnoses than any other.*

![Close-up of a senior cat's face](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1771159207144-8cc3d5b35d03?auto=format&fit=crop&w=1200&q=80)
*Cats age well outwardly. The changes happen where you cannot see them.*
## When a cat becomes senior

| Stage | Age | What it means |
|---|---|---|
| Mature | 7–10 years | Metabolism slows; weight starts to drift |
| Senior | 11–14 years | Screening should become routine |
| Geriatric | 15+ years | Most cats have at least one chronic condition |
Indoor cats routinely reach their late teens. Those years are worth planning for rather than reacting to.
## The four conditions to expect

**Chronic kidney disease.** Extremely common in older cats. Signs are drinking more, urinating more, weight loss and a dull coat. It is progressive and manageable, and caught early it is manageable for years.
**Hyperthyroidism.** An overactive thyroid. The classic picture is a cat that is **losing weight while eating ravenously**, often restless or unusually vocal at night. Very treatable.
**Arthritis.** Most cats over twelve have arthritic changes on X-ray. They rarely limp. They stop jumping instead.
**Diabetes.** More common in overweight and neutered males. Drinking, urinating and weight loss again — which is why these signs always mean bloodwork, never a guess.
> Three unrelated diseases share the same early signs: drinking more, urinating more, losing weight. That overlap is exactly why the answer is a blood test rather than a theory.
## The twice-yearly rule
From about eleven, aim for a check-up **every six months**. A year is a long time in a cat's life, and these conditions move faster than annual visits catch.
A useful senior screen includes:

- Weight, compared against the last visit
- Blood pressure — hypertension is common and can cause sudden blindness
- Blood biochemistry and a full blood count
- **Total T4** for thyroid function
- Urinalysis, which often flags kidney change before blood does

![A cat being held calmly](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1596272875729-ed2ff7d6d9c5?auto=format&fit=crop&w=1200&q=80)
*Weight is the single most useful number you can track at home.*
## Weigh the cat monthly

A kitchen scale and a note on your phone will do. In an older cat, **losing 5% of body weight is significant**, and that is only 200 g on a 4 kg cat — invisible by eye, invisible by feel, obvious on a scale.
Weight loss is the earliest sign of nearly everything on the list above.
## Adapting the home
Old cats do not ask for help. They just stop doing things.

- **Litter tray with a low entry.** A high-sided tray is a hurdle for a stiff cat, and stepping over it is often the real reason for accidents beside it.
- **More trays, on every floor.** A long walk is a deterrent at fifteen.
- **Steps or a stool** up to the favourite windowsill or bed.
- **Raise the food and water bowls** slightly to ease neck and shoulder strain.
- **Warm, draught-free beds.** Arthritic joints stiffen in the cold.
- **Non-slip rugs** on wooden or tiled floors, where old claws lose grip.
- **Help with grooming.** Stiff cats cannot reach the lower back, and mats form there first.
## Food in later life
There is no single senior diet, because the right one depends on the diagnosis.

- **Healthy senior:** highly digestible protein, plenty of it. The old advice to restrict protein in all older cats is outdated and risks muscle loss.
- **Diagnosed kidney disease:** a prescription renal diet, which restricts phosphorus. This is one of the few dietary changes with strong evidence behind it.
- **Losing weight:** more calories and more palatability, warmed slightly to lift the aroma.
- **Always:** more moisture. Ageing kidneys benefit from every millilitre.
## The short version
Do not explain a change by age. Age is when things go wrong, not the reason they do. Weigh monthly, screen twice a year, and treat any new behaviour as information.
*General guidance only. Any change in an older cat's drinking, appetite, weight or mobility deserves a veterinary visit.*

title: Hairballs: What Is Normal and What Is Not
excerpt: An occasional hairball is housekeeping. A weekly one is a symptom.
body: *Most owners treat hairballs as a fact of cat ownership. Frequent ones usually mean something else is going on.*

![A cat licking its paw](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1511275539165-cc46b1ee89bf?auto=format&fit=crop&w=1200&q=80)
*Cats spend a large share of waking hours grooming. All that fur goes somewhere.*
## Where they come from
A cat's tongue is covered in backward-facing keratin spines called papillae. They work like a comb, and they make it nearly impossible to spit anything out — whatever the tongue catches goes down.

Most swallowed hair passes through and leaves in the faeces. Occasionally it gathers in the stomach, forms a mass, and comes back up. The proper name is a **trichobezoar**, and the sausage shape comes from the oesophagus, not the stomach.
## How often is too often

| Frequency | Reading |
|---|---|
| A few times a year | Normal, especially in long-haired cats and during moult |
| Monthly | Worth a mention at the next check-up |
| Weekly or more | Not normal — investigate |
| Repeated retching with nothing produced | **See a vet promptly** |
> A cat that brings up hairballs often is usually either grooming too much or moving food through too slowly. Both are medical questions, not grooming ones.
## What frequent hairballs usually mean

**Overgrooming.** A cat swallowing unusual amounts of hair is pulling unusual amounts out. The causes are itch and stress: fleas, food allergy, atopic skin disease, pain in a specific spot, or anxiety. Look for thin patches, especially on the belly, flanks and inner thighs, where a cat can reach easily.

**Reduced gut motility.** Inflammatory bowel disease and other chronic gut conditions slow transit, so hair that should pass through sits and clumps. Often paired with intermittent vomiting, soft stools or slow weight loss.

**Simply a lot of coat.** Persians, Maine Coons and other long-haired breeds genuinely produce more, and moulting seasons make it worse. This is the benign explanation, and it is a diagnosis of exclusion.
## What actually helps

1. **Brush more, and brush properly.** Hair on the brush is hair not in the stomach. Daily for long-haired cats, twice weekly for short.
2. **Treat for fleas year round.** Flea allergy is the commonest cause of overgrooming, and you will not always see fleas.
3. **Add moisture.** Wet food and a well-hydrated gut move hair along better.
4. **Fibre.** Small amounts of plain pumpkin, or a hairball-control diet with added fibre, help transit.
5. **Hairball pastes** lubricate rather than dissolve. Useful occasionally, not a fix for a weekly problem.
## When it is an emergency
Rarely, a mass becomes an intestinal obstruction. Call a vet **immediately** if you see:

- Repeated unproductive retching
- Vomiting that will not stop, or no food kept down for 24 hours
- A hard, distended or painful belly
- Lethargy with no appetite
- No stool for more than two days
Obstruction is surgical, and it does not resolve on its own.
## The short version
An occasional hairball is normal. A regular one is your cat telling you it is grooming too much or digesting too slowly, and both are worth a conversation with your vet.
*General guidance only. Persistent vomiting in a cat is never normal, hairball or not.*

title: Is Your Cat Overweight? How to Actually Tell
excerpt: Roughly half of pet cats carry too much weight, and most owners cannot see it.
body: *Half of the cats in most surveyed households are overweight. Roughly the same share of owners describe their cat as "just right."*

![A ginger cat loafing on the floor](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1519052537078-e6302a4968d4?auto=format&fit=crop&w=1200&q=80)
*Fluff hides a lot. Your hands are more honest than your eyes.*
## The hands-on test
Vets use a **body condition score**, usually out of nine, where 5 is ideal. You can run the same three checks at home in under a minute.

### 1. Ribs
Run your palms along both sides of the chest.

- **Ideal:** you feel the ribs easily under a thin layer, like the back of your knuckles
- **Overweight:** you have to press to find them, like the back of your hand
- **Underweight:** they feel sharp and prominent

### 2. Waist from above
Stand over the cat and look down. You should see a definite narrowing behind the ribs. A straight or bulging outline is excess weight.

### 3. Profile from the side
There should be an upward tuck from the ribcage to the hind legs. A belly that hangs level with or below the chest is a warning.
> **The primordial pouch is not fat.** The loose flap of skin along the lower belly is normal anatomy, present on lean cats too, and it swings when they run. Judge by ribs and waist, not the pouch.
## Why it matters more in cats

| Risk | Effect of excess weight |
|---|---|
| Diabetes mellitus | Several times more likely |
| Arthritis | More load on already ageing joints |
| Urinary disease | Less movement, less drinking, more sitting |
| Grooming | Cannot reach the back — dandruff and mats follow |
| Hepatic lipidosis | Crash dieting can trigger liver failure |
| Lifespan | Consistently shorter in overweight animals |
That last row is the one that matters most, and the one crash-dieting owners get wrong.
## The rule that must not be broken

**Never starve a cat thin.** A cat in sudden calorie deficit mobilises fat faster than its liver can process, and overweight cats are the most at risk. The result is **hepatic lipidosis**, a life-threatening liver failure that can start after only a few days of not eating.
Safe loss is **1–2% of body weight per week**. On a 6 kg cat that is 60–120 g. Slow is the entire point.
## What actually works

1. **Measure the food.** Weigh the daily ration on a kitchen scale. Cups and eyeballing are the main cause of drift.
2. **Start from calories, not packet guidance.** Packet portions assume an active, unneutered adult. Most house cats need less.
3. **Switch some ration to wet food.** More volume and more water for the same calories.
4. **Count the treats.** They must stay under 10% of daily calories, and they rarely do.
5. **Feed separately** in multi-cat homes, or the thin one subsidises the fat one.
6. **Make food work.** Puzzle feeders and food balls slow eating and add activity.
7. **Play twice a day**, five to ten minutes, with a wand toy. Chase, catch, feed.
8. **Weigh monthly** and record it. Without numbers you cannot see progress.
## Rough daily calories
Very rough guidance for an average neutered indoor adult, before any vet adjustment:

| Target weight | Approx. kcal per day |
|---|---|
| 3 kg | 160 |
| 4 kg | 200 |
| 5 kg | 240 |
| 6 kg | 270 |
For weight loss, work from the **target** weight, not the current one, and ask your vet to confirm the number.
## The short version
Feel the ribs, look for a waist, weigh monthly. If the cat needs to lose weight, do it slowly and with your vet — a fast diet is more dangerous than the extra kilo.
*General guidance only. Plan any weight-loss programme with your veterinary practice, especially for a cat that has stopped eating.*

title: Litter Tray Red Flags Every Owner Should Know
excerpt: The tray is the best diagnostic tool in your home, and it is free.
body: *Cats hide almost everything. What they cannot hide is what they leave in the tray.*

![A cat sitting in a litter box](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1727510153658-643787acb16a?auto=format&fit=crop&w=1200&q=80)
*Thirty seconds of attention a day catches problems weeks early.*
## The emergency, first
**A male cat straining in the tray and producing little or no urine is a medical emergency.** A urethral blockage can be fatal within 24 to 48 hours.
It is easily mistaken for constipation, because the posture is identical. If you are unsure, treat it as a blockage and phone the vet.
Signs:

- Repeated trips with nothing produced
- Straining, crying or vocalising in the tray
- Licking the genitals persistently
- Blood-tinged drips
- Vomiting, hiding, collapse in later stages
Males are at far greater risk because the urethra is longer and narrower. Females get the same disease and rarely block.
## What to check daily

| What you see | What it may mean |
|---|---|
| Sudden small clumps | Drinking less, or urinating small volumes frequently |
| Very large clumps, more of them | Increased urination — kidney disease, diabetes, hyperthyroidism |
| Blood in urine | Cystitis, crystals, infection |
| Straining with little output | **Emergency — see above** |
| Hard, dry, pellet-like stool | Constipation or dehydration |
| Loose stool for more than 48 hours | Diet change, parasites, inflammatory disease |
| Nothing at all for 48 hours | Obstruction or blockage |
| Going next to the tray | Medical until proven otherwise |
> Cats do not urinate outside the tray out of spite. Punishing it guarantees you will miss the disease underneath.

![A cat resting on a light surface](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1603104010974-de673b7c5674?auto=format&fit=crop&w=1200&q=80)
*Cats associate pain with place. A tray that hurt once becomes a tray to avoid.*
## Why scoopable litter is a diagnostic tool

Clumping litter lets you see volume, which is the single most useful number the tray gives you. More or larger clumps mean more urine, and more urine is the shared early sign of the three big older-cat diseases.
Two habits make it work:

- **Scoop at least once a day** and glance at what you remove
- **Keep a rough count.** "Two clumps became five over a fortnight" is real clinical information
## Setup that prevents problems

- **One tray per cat, plus one spare.** Two cats need three trays.
- **Spread them out.** Two trays side by side count as one to a cat.
- **Uncovered, large and open.** Hoods trap odour and block escape routes, and many cats dislike them. A tray should be about **1.5 times the cat's body length**.
- **Unscented, fine-grained clumping litter** is preferred in most preference studies.
- **About 5 cm depth**, scooped daily, fully changed and washed weekly.
- **Quiet location**, away from the food, the water and the washing machine.
- **Low entry for older cats.** Stiff joints turn a high side into a barrier.
## When a healthy cat starts missing the tray
Once your vet has ruled out disease, work through the physical causes before you consider behaviour:

1. Has the litter type or brand changed?
2. Is it clean enough, by the cat's standard rather than yours?
3. Has anything frightening happened near it — a noisy appliance, another pet, a child?
4. Is a second cat guarding the route?
5. Is it too far, too high, or up a flight of stairs for an older cat?
## The short version
Look in the tray every day. Volume, frequency and effort are the three things worth noticing, and a straining male cat means the phone, not the internet.
*General guidance only. Suspected urinary blockage is an emergency — contact a vet immediately.*

title: The Preventive Care Calendar
excerpt: Vaccines, parasites and check-ups, laid out by age so nothing slips.
body: *Most of what keeps a cat healthy is scheduled, unglamorous and easy to forget.*

![A kitten being examined by a vet](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1725409796872-8b41e8eca929?auto=format&fit=crop&w=1200&q=80)
*The first year sets the schedule for every year after it.*
## Vaccines: core and non-core
**Core** vaccines are recommended for every cat, indoor or not. Indoor-only cats are still exposed — viruses travel on shoes, hands and open windows.

| Vaccine | Protects against | Who needs it |
|---|---|---|
| **FVRCP** | Feline herpesvirus, calicivirus, panleukopenia | Every cat |
| **Rabies** | Rabies | Every cat where required by law |
| **FeLV** | Feline leukaemia virus | Kittens, and any cat with outdoor access |
Panleukopenia is the one that justifies the whole schedule. It is highly contagious, environmentally durable and frequently fatal in kittens.
**Non-core** vaccines, such as FIV or chlamydia, depend on lifestyle and local risk. Your vet decides these, not the internet.
## Kittens: the first six months

1. **6–8 weeks** — first FVRCP; first deworming
2. **10–12 weeks** — second FVRCP; FeLV course begins; deworming repeated
3. **14–16 weeks** — final FVRCP; FeLV completed; rabies where required
4. **4–6 months** — neutering, and a check that the adult teeth are coming in properly
> A kitten is not protected until the **final** dose of the series. Maternal antibodies block earlier ones unpredictably, which is exactly why there are three.
Deworm kittens every two weeks from three weeks old until three months, then monthly to six months. Roundworms pass through the mother's milk, so assume they are present.
## Adults: one to ten years

- **Annual health check**, including weight, teeth, heart and coat
- **Vaccine boosters** on your vet's schedule, typically every one to three years by component
- **Flea and tick prevention** all year, including indoor cats — fleas arrive on trouser legs
- **Deworming** two to four times a year, more for hunters
- **Weigh at home every one to two months**

![A cat being held calmly by its owner](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1596272875729-ed2ff7d6d9c5?auto=format&fit=crop&w=1200&q=80)
*Yearly for adults, twice yearly from about eleven.*
## Seniors: eleven and up
Move to a **six-month** cycle, and add screening:

- Blood biochemistry and full blood count
- **Total T4** for thyroid
- Urinalysis, which flags kidney change early
- Blood pressure, since hypertension can cause sudden blindness
- A proper look at the mouth
## Parasites worth knowing

**Fleas.** The most common cause of itching and overgrooming. Flea allergy needs only a single bite. Treat every cat in the household, and treat the environment as well, since most of the population lives in the carpet rather than on the cat.
**Ticks.** Outdoor cats. Remove with a tick hook, twisting rather than pulling, and never with oil or a flame.
**Worms.** Roundworms and tapeworms are common; tapeworm usually arrives via fleas, so flea control is worm control. Rice-like segments near the tail are the classic sign.
**Ear mites.** Dark, crumbly discharge and furious scratching. Common in kittens and rescues, and highly contagious between pets.
> **Never use a dog flea product on a cat.** Permethrin, common in canine spot-ons, is severely toxic to cats and kills them every year.
## A microchip is preventive care too
Register it, and **keep the details current**. A chip with an old phone number is a chip that does nothing. Check the registration each time you move house.
## The short version
Three FVRCP doses in kittenhood, annual checks through adulthood, twice-yearly with bloodwork from eleven, and year-round flea control for every cat regardless of whether it goes outside.
*General guidance only. Vaccination and parasite schedules vary by country and lifestyle — your vet's plan takes precedence.*

title: What Your Cat's Coat Is Telling You
excerpt: A dull coat is rarely a grooming problem. It is usually a health one.
body: *Cats spend a significant share of their waking hours grooming. When the coat goes wrong, the cause is usually somewhere else.*

![A cat grooming itself on a ledge](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1771088728009-f6d1a8d7e0fa?auto=format&fit=crop&w=1200&q=80)
*Grooming is one of the first things a cat gives up when it feels unwell.*
## Reading the coat

| What you see | Likely cause |
|---|---|
| Dull, greasy, clumped | Grooming has stopped — pain, illness, obesity or dental disease |
| Dandruff on the lower back | Cannot twist to reach it: arthritis or excess weight |
| Matting behind the shoulders | Reduced flexibility, or long coat plus insufficient brushing |
| Thin patch on belly or inner thigh | Overgrooming from itch, allergy or stress |
| Bald patches with broken hairs | Overgrooming rather than hair loss |
| Bald patches with intact skin | Hormonal or fungal — needs a vet |
| Sudden heavy shedding | Stress, season change, or illness |
| Black specks at the tail base | Flea dirt, even if you see no fleas |
> A cat's coat is a free daily health report. Dullness is the earliest and most commonly ignored line in it.
## Overgrooming versus hair loss
The distinction matters, and you can make it yourself. Look closely at a thin patch.

- **Broken, stubbly hairs at different lengths** — the cat is barbering it off. Look for itch or pain.
- **Smooth skin with no stubble** — the hair is falling out. Think hormonal disease or ringworm.

The commonest cause of feline overgrooming is **flea allergy**, and a single bite is enough. You will often never see a flea on a fastidious cat. The second commonest is stress. Both are treatable; guessing between them is not.
## How to brush, by coat type
**Short-haired cats:** twice weekly is enough. A rubber curry brush or grooming mitt lifts loose hair without pulling.
**Long-haired cats:** daily, without exception. A metal comb is the essential tool, because a slicker brush glides over the surface while a mat forms underneath.
Work in this order:

1. Start where the cat likes being touched — usually cheeks and chin
2. Move along the back with the direction of the coat
3. Do the **danger zones** last: armpits, behind the ears, the trousers at the back legs, and the lower back
4. Stop before the cat wants you to. Two short sessions beat one long argument

![A relaxed tabby resting](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1518791841217-8f162f1e1131?auto=format&fit=crop&w=1200&q=80)
*Brushing removes hair that would otherwise be swallowed, which means fewer hairballs.*
## Mats
A mat is not a tangle. It is felted hair pulling on living skin, and underneath it the skin is often red and sore.

- **Never cut a mat out with scissors.** Cat skin is thin and mobile, it lifts into the mat, and lacerations from this are a routine emergency presentation.
- Work small mats apart with fingers and a comb, holding the hair at the base so you are not pulling the skin.
- Large or close-set mats are a job for a groomer or vet with clippers, sometimes under sedation.
- A heavily matted cat is usually a cat that stopped grooming. Ask why.
## Claws, ears and eyes

- **Claws.** Trim only the clear tip, staying well clear of the pink quick. Indoor and older cats need it most, since they wear claws down less.
- **Ears.** Should be clean and nearly odourless. Dark crumbly wax means mites; a yeasty smell means infection. Never use a cotton bud inside the canal.
- **Eyes.** A little clear discharge is normal in flat-faced breeds. Coloured discharge, squinting or a visible third eyelid needs a vet.
## The short version
Brush regularly, and treat a coat change as a symptom rather than a cosmetic issue. A cat that has stopped grooming is telling you something hurts.
*General guidance only. Sudden coat changes, bald patches or persistent scratching need veterinary assessment.*

title: How to Take a Cat to the Vet Without the Fight
excerpt: The carrier is the whole problem, and it is fixable in two weeks.
body: *Owners skip appointments because the journey is worse than the worry. That is a solvable problem.*

![A person holding a calm tabby cat](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1596272875729-ed2ff7d6d9c5?auto=format&fit=crop&w=1200&q=80)
*A cat that is calm on arrival gets a better examination.*
## Why cats find it so hard

A cat's security comes from **territory and predictability**. A vet visit removes both at once: an unfamiliar box, a moving vehicle, a room smelling of dogs and other cats' fear pheromones, then handling by a stranger.

Cats also learn associations fast and unlearn them slowly. If the carrier only ever appears before something unpleasant, the carrier itself becomes the threat. Most of the struggle happens before you leave the house.
## Fix the carrier first
This is the highest-value change, and it takes about two weeks.

1. **Leave the carrier out permanently**, door removed or tied open, in a room the cat uses.
2. **Make it comfortable** — a soft blanket, ideally one that already smells of home.
3. **Feed near it**, then in the doorway, then inside.
4. **Drop treats in** at random times so the cat finds them on its own.
5. **Never** use it as punishment or a way to catch the cat for anything else.

Choose a **hard carrier that opens from the top and has a removable lid**. It matters more than it sounds: a cat can be lifted out gently, or examined sitting in the base rather than being tipped out of a front door.
> A cat dragged out of a carrier starts the consultation frightened. A cat examined in the bottom half of its own carrier often stays calm throughout.
## The day itself

- **Withhold breakfast** if your vet agrees, so treats work as currency and car sickness is less likely
- **Spray a synthetic feline pheromone** on the bedding 15 minutes before, not while the cat is inside
- **Cover the carrier** with a towel to reduce visual stimulation
- **Secure it in the car** with a seatbelt, in the footwell or on the seat, never in the boot
- **Drive smoothly** and skip the radio
- **In the waiting room**, keep the carrier off the floor and away from dogs. Ask for a cat-only area, or wait in the car and ask to be called
## At the practice
Ask for what you need. Good practices expect it.

- Request a **cat-only or quiet consulting room**
- Ask that the **lid be removed** rather than the cat pulled out
- Let the cat come out in its own time when the situation allows
- Bring a familiar towel to place on the table
- Ask about **gabapentin or another pre-visit medication** for genuinely fearful cats. This is routine, evidence-backed, and not a failure
## Getting a reluctant cat into the carrier
When you have not had time to prepare:

1. Close the door of the room first, so there is nowhere to bolt
2. Put the carrier **on end**, opening upward
3. Wrap the cat gently in a towel, supporting the chest and back legs
4. Lower it in **rear end first** — a cat resists forwards far more than backwards
5. Close the door and set it flat
Never chase a cat around the house. You will lose, and you will make the next attempt harder.
## Multi-cat households
Cats returning from the vet smell wrong, and their housemates may react with hissing or aggression. This is normal and usually short-lived.

- Bring the returning cat home in its carrier and let it out in a quiet room
- Give it an hour to re-groom and smell like itself again
- Reintroduce calmly, with food, rather than forcing contact
## The short version
Leave the carrier out year round, choose one with a removable top, and ask your practice for a quiet room. Most of a vet visit's stress is logistics, and logistics can be changed.
*General guidance only. Ask your veterinary practice about pre-visit anti-anxiety medication for cats that find appointments genuinely distressing.*

title: Wet Food or Dry Food? The Honest Comparison
excerpt: One wins on moisture and protein, the other on cost and convenience.
body: *The debate is usually argued as though one is food and the other is poison. Neither is true.*

![A cat beside a food bowl](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1645773619957-ec1d128d0aa2?auto=format&fit=crop&w=1200&q=80)
*Most cats do best on a mix, weighted toward wet.*
## The single biggest difference
**Moisture.** Wet food is roughly 75–80% water. Dry food is around 6–10%.

That one number drives most of the real advantages. A cat's thirst drive is weak, inherited from desert ancestors that got water from prey. Cats on dry food do drink more, but generally not enough more to close the gap — which matters for urinary and kidney health across a lifetime.
## Side by side

| | Wet food | Dry food |
|---|---|---|
| Moisture | 75–80% | 6–10% |
| Protein, dry matter | Usually higher | Usually lower |
| Carbohydrate | Usually lower | Higher — starch is needed to form kibble |
| Calorie density | Low, so more volume per calorie | High, easy to overfeed |
| Cost per calorie | Higher | Lower |
| Free feeding | Unsafe to leave out | Possible, though rarely advisable |
| Dental effect | Neutral | **Neutral** — standard kibble does not clean teeth |
| Shelf life once open | 24 hours refrigerated | Weeks |

> The idea that dry food cleans teeth is the most persistent myth in cat nutrition. Standard kibble shatters on contact, above the gum line where disease actually starts. Only specific dental diets with larger, fibrous kibble do anything measurable.
## Where wet food genuinely wins

- **Urinary health.** More dilute urine, fewer crystals, less irritation.
- **Weight control.** More volume per calorie, so a satisfying meal costs less.
- **Protein.** Typically higher on a dry matter basis, and cats are obligate carnivores.
- **Older cats.** Easier to eat with dental disease, easier on ageing kidneys.
- **Palatability.** Aroma and texture matter to a cat that has gone off its food.
## Where dry food genuinely wins

- **Cost.** Often substantially cheaper per calorie.
- **Convenience.** No refrigeration, no spoilage, travels well.
- **Puzzle feeding.** Works in food balls and puzzle toys that add activity.
- **Timed feeders.** Practical for long working days.
## Comparing labels fairly
You cannot read the two panels side by side. Convert both to **dry matter basis** first:

```
Dry matter % = (as-fed %) / (100 - moisture %) × 100
```

| | Wet food | Dry food |
|---|---|---|
| Protein as printed | 10% | 32% |
| Moisture | 78% | 8% |
| **Protein, dry matter** | **45.5%** | **34.8%** |
The wet food that looked far weaker is comfortably ahead.
## A practical middle path
For most healthy adult cats:

1. **At least one wet meal a day**, ideally two
2. **Dry food measured, not free-fed** — weigh the daily amount
3. **Use dry in puzzle feeders** so it earns activity
4. **Fresh water always available**, away from the food bowl
5. **Treats under 10%** of daily calories, counted from the total
Cats with a history of urinary blockage, crystals or kidney disease should generally be on **wet food primarily**, and that decision belongs with your vet.
## Feeding safely

- Do not leave wet food out more than an hour or two in a warm room
- Refrigerate an opened tin, covered, for no more than 24 hours
- Serve at room temperature — cats reject cold food, and aroma drives appetite
- Store dry food sealed in its original bag; the fat oxidises and goes stale in the open
## The short version
Wet food is better for hydration, weight and urinary health. Dry food is cheaper and more convenient. A measured mix, leaning wet, suits most cats — and the dental argument for kibble does not hold.
*General guidance only. Cats with kidney, urinary or diabetic disease need a diet chosen with their vet.*

title: How Much Should My Cat Actually Eat?
excerpt: Packet guidance is a starting point, and usually a generous one.
body: *The number on the packet assumes a cat that does not live in your house.*

![A cat eating from a ceramic bowl](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1580238169544-86bf7cd8c84c?auto=format&fit=crop&w=1200&q=80)
*A kitchen scale removes almost all of the guesswork.*
## Start with calories, not cups
Feeding guides are built around an average active adult, often unneutered. Most house cats are neutered, indoor and considerably less active, and need meaningfully less.
Rough daily energy for a **neutered indoor adult at a healthy weight**:

| Body weight | Approx. kcal per day |
|---|---|
| 3 kg | 160 |
| 4 kg | 200 |
| 5 kg | 240 |
| 6 kg | 270 |
Adjust from there:

- **Active or outdoor cat:** add 10–20%
- **Older, sedentary or arthritic:** subtract 10%
- **Kitten:** roughly two to three times adult maintenance per kilo of body weight
- **Pregnant or nursing:** substantially more, guided by your vet
- **For weight loss:** calculate from the **target** weight, never the current one
## Turn calories into grams
Every complete food prints its energy density, usually as **kcal per 100 g** or per cup. If it is not on the packet it is on the manufacturer's website.

```
Grams per day = (daily kcal target) / (kcal per 100 g) × 100
```
A 4 kg cat needing 200 kcal, on a food with 380 kcal per 100 g:
That is a strikingly small pile of kibble, and it is the usual moment owners realise they have been overfeeding.
> **Weigh the food.** A scoop of kibble varies by up to a third depending on how it settles. Grams do not.
## How often to feed
Cats are natural grazers, evolved to eat many small meals. In practice:

- **Two to four measured meals a day** suits most adults
- **Kittens under six months** need three or four meals
- **Free feeding** is workable only for a cat that self-regulates well, and most do not
- **Multi-cat homes** should feed separately, or the confident cat eats twice
Whatever the pattern, the **daily total** is what matters. Split it however fits your day.
## Counting treats honestly
Treats belong inside the daily total, not on top of it, and should stay under **10% of daily calories**. For a 4 kg cat that is about 20 kcal — a handful of small treats at most.
Also counted: dental chews, lickable tubes, the milk in the cereal bowl, and anything that falls off a plate.
## Signs you have it wrong
**Too much**

- Ribs hard to feel, waist disappearing from above
- Steady monthly weight gain
- Food left in the bowl and still gaining
**Too little**

- Ribs, spine and hips prominent
- Persistent food seeking, counter surfing, yowling before meals
- Weight loss without a diet change — **always a vet visit**, since it is the leading sign of hyperthyroidism, kidney disease and diabetes
## Weigh the cat, not just the food
Once a month, on a kitchen scale, and write it down. Body weight is the only honest verdict on whether the number you chose is right.
In an older cat, a **5% loss is significant** — 200 g on a 4 kg cat. That is invisible by eye and obvious on a scale.
## The short version
Work out the calories, convert to grams, weigh the food and weigh the cat monthly. Adjust by what the scale says, not by what the bowl looks like.
*General guidance only. Confirm calorie targets with your vet, particularly for kittens, seniors, pregnant cats and any cat on a weight-loss plan.*

title: Why a Cat Cannot Be Vegetarian
excerpt: This is not a preference. It is a set of missing enzymes.
body: *Dogs are omnivores and can be argued about. Cats are obligate carnivores, and the argument ends at their biochemistry.*

![A board of raw meats](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1607623814075-e51df1bdc82f?auto=format&fit=crop&w=1200&q=80)
*Cats evolved eating whole small animals, and their metabolism never developed a plan B.*
## What "obligate carnivore" means

Over millions of years eating almost nothing but meat, cats lost metabolic pathways they no longer needed. Once a pathway is gone, the nutrient it produced has to arrive ready-made in food — and in practice that means from animal tissue.
This is not a mild preference. Several of these deficiencies cause irreversible damage.
## The five things cats cannot make

### Taurine
An amino acid found almost exclusively in animal tissue. Cats cannot synthesise enough, and deficiency causes **irreversible retinal degeneration leading to blindness** and **dilated cardiomyopathy**, a heart failure that can be fatal. The link was only identified in the 1980s, after cats fed taurine-poor commercial diets began going blind.

### Preformed vitamin A
Humans and dogs convert beta-carotene from plants into vitamin A. Cats lack sufficient enzyme activity to do it. They need **retinol**, from liver and other animal tissue.

### Arachidonic acid
An essential fatty acid for skin, coat, reproduction and inflammatory regulation. Other species make it from plant-derived linoleic acid. Cats cannot, and it is found only in animal fat.

### Vitamin B12 and niacin
Cats have high requirements and limited ability to produce niacin from tryptophan. Both come most reliably from meat.

### High-quality protein, continuously
A cat's liver runs protein-processing enzymes at a **constantly high rate** rather than adjusting to intake. It keeps burning protein even when little is coming in, which is why cats need more dietary protein than dogs and why fasting is dangerous for them.
> This is also why a cat that stops eating gets into trouble so fast. Within a few days it can develop **hepatic lipidosis**, a life-threatening liver failure.

![A cat waiting by its bowl](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1558993457-4bc6ec2c3734?auto=format&fit=crop&w=1200&q=80)
*Enthusiasm for meat is not spoiled behaviour. It is a metabolic requirement.*
## What about synthetic supplements?
It is chemically possible to synthesise taurine, retinol, arachidonic acid and B12, and a small number of vegan cat foods do exactly that. It is worth being straight about where the evidence sits.

- Synthetic taurine is genuinely used in **all** commercial cat food, including meat-based, because processing destroys some of what was there.
- The harder problems are the ones nobody lists: protein digestibility and amino acid balance, palatability, urinary pH, and the long-term data that does not yet exist at scale.
- Reported deficiencies in vegan-fed cats have historically involved home-prepared diets and inadequate supplementation.

If someone chooses this route for ethical reasons, it must be a **complete, tested commercial diet** with veterinary supervision and periodic bloodwork including taurine levels. Home-made plant-based cat food is not a safe project.
## Practical consequences

- Read the ingredient list for **named animal proteins at the top**
- Treat high-carbohydrate foods with suspicion; cats have limited carbohydrate-processing machinery
- Do not let a cat go without food for more than 24 hours
- Never apply human or canine dietary philosophy to a cat
## The short version
A cat's body outsourced several essential jobs to the animals it eats. You can supplement around the edges, but the underlying biology is not negotiable.
*General guidance only. Never place a cat on a plant-based diet without veterinary supervision and regular blood monitoring.*

title: Taurine and the Nutrients Cats Cannot Make
excerpt: Six nutrients a cat must eat ready-made, and what happens when it does not.
body: *Every complete cat food is built around a short list of things a cat's body gave up producing.*

![A whole fish on a wooden board](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1611171711912-e3f6b536f532?auto=format&fit=crop&w=1200&q=80)
*Fish and shellfish are rich in taurine. So are heart and other organ meats.*
## Taurine, and the discovery that changed pet food

Taurine is an amino acid concentrated in heart muscle, retina and brain. Most mammals make enough from other amino acids. Cats make very little, and they lose it constantly, because they use taurine to make bile salts and cannot recycle it efficiently.

In the 1980s, cats fed certain commercial diets began developing **dilated cardiomyopathy**, a heart that stretches and weakens until it fails. Researchers traced it to taurine deficiency. Manufacturers reformulated, and the disease became rare almost overnight.
The other deficiency sign is **central retinal degeneration** — a slow, painless loss of vision that is **permanent** once it happens.

| Source | Taurine content |
|---|---|
| Heart, especially poultry heart | Very high |
| Shellfish and dark fish muscle | High |
| Red meat | Moderate |
| Chicken breast | Lower |
| Plants | Essentially none |
| Boiled meat | **Reduced** — taurine leaches into the water |
> That last row is why home cooking is riskier than it looks. Boil chicken for a cat and you pour a good share of the taurine down the sink. Use the cooking liquid.
## The rest of the list

### Preformed vitamin A
Cats cannot convert plant beta-carotene efficiently. They need **retinol** from liver and animal tissue. Deficiency affects vision, skin and immunity — but excess is also toxic, which is why liver should be a small part of a diet and never the bulk of it.

### Arachidonic acid
An omega-6 fatty acid cats cannot make from plant precursors. Needed for skin barrier function, coat, kidney function and reproduction. Found in animal fat.

### Vitamin B12 (cobalamin)
Absorbed in the last section of the small intestine. Cats have a short half-life for it, so chronic gut disease causes deficiency quickly. Injectable B12 is a common part of treating feline inflammatory bowel disease.

### Niacin (B3)
Most mammals make some from tryptophan. Cats' enzyme pathway diverts it elsewhere, so dietary niacin is essential.

### Protein, at a high and constant rate
A cat's liver does not dial protein breakdown down when intake falls. This is why cats need more protein than dogs and why **fasting is genuinely dangerous** for them.
## What this means in practice

1. **Choose complete and balanced food.** Every one is supplemented with taurine, because processing destroys part of what was in the meat.
2. **Treat home-cooked food as incomplete** unless a veterinary nutritionist formulated it. Plain chicken and rice is not a diet.
3. **If you cook, keep the cooking liquid** and serve it with the meat.
4. **Do not overdo liver.** A little is valuable; a lot causes vitamin A toxicity and painful bone changes.
5. **Do not feed dog food.** It is not supplemented for feline taurine, vitamin A or arachidonic acid needs.
6. **Raw fish is a specific risk.** Some contains thiaminase, an enzyme that destroys vitamin B1, and thiamine deficiency causes neurological damage.
## Signs of long-term deficiency
These develop slowly and are easy to miss:

- Declining night vision, bumping into things, dilated pupils
- Lethargy, breathlessness or a heart murmur
- Poor coat, flaky skin, slow healing
- Weight and muscle loss despite eating
- Poor growth in kittens
By the time retinal damage is visible on examination, it cannot be reversed.
## The short version
Taurine, vitamin A, arachidonic acid, B12, niacin and abundant protein all have to arrive ready-made in a cat's food. That is precisely what "complete and balanced" on the label is certifying.
*General guidance only. Home-prepared diets should be formulated by a veterinary nutritionist.*

title: Foods That Are Toxic to Cats
excerpt: Some are famous, some are in your kitchen right now, and one is a houseplant.
body: *A cat is small, and its liver processes some compounds far less efficiently than ours. Dose matters more than it does for us.*

![A pile of onions](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1508747703725-719777637510?auto=format&fit=crop&w=1200&q=80)
*Onion and garlic are the most common accidental poisonings, usually hidden inside cooked leftovers.*
## The serious list

### Onion, garlic, leek, chives, shallot
All members of the *Allium* family damage feline red blood cells, causing **haemolytic anaemia**. Cats are **more sensitive than dogs**, and cooking does not help — powdered forms are the most concentrated of all.
The realistic risk is not a whole onion. It is gravy, stock, baby food, stuffing and leftover casserole.

### Lilies — not food, but the top emergency
Every part of a true lily is severely toxic to cats, including the pollen and the vase water. **A cat that walks past a lily and grooms the pollen off its fur can go into acute kidney failure.**
If you own a cat, do not have lilies in the house. If exposure is suspected, that is an immediate emergency.

### Chocolate, coffee, tea, energy drinks
Theobromine and caffeine. Cats are rarely tempted by chocolate, but ingestion causes tremors, racing heart, seizures. Dark and baking chocolate are the most dangerous.

### Grapes and raisins
Documented kidney failure in dogs; the mechanism remains unclear and cats are treated as at risk. Watch for raisins in baked goods.

### Alcohol and raw yeast dough
Cats are tiny and there is no safe amount. Raw dough is doubly dangerous: it expands in the stomach and ferments into alcohol.

### Xylitol (birch sugar)
In sugar-free gum, sweets, some peanut butters and **some human toothpastes**. The strongest evidence for severe toxicity is in dogs, but it should be kept away from cats entirely.

### Raw fish, in quantity
Some species contain **thiaminase**, which destroys vitamin B1. Chronic feeding causes neurological damage. Cooking deactivates it.

### Bones, especially cooked
Cooked bones splinter. Perforation and obstruction are surgical emergencies.
## The "not toxic, still a bad idea" list

| Food | Problem |
|---|---|
| Cow's milk | Most adult cats are lactose intolerant — diarrhoea |
| Raw egg white | Avidin binds biotin; also a salmonella risk |
| Tuna as a staple | Nutritionally unbalanced, and cats fixate on it |
| Liver in quantity | Vitamin A toxicity, causing painful bone changes |
| Salty snacks, crisps, cured meat | Sodium load a small animal does not need |
| Fat trimmings | Pancreatitis risk |
| Dog food | Not supplemented for feline taurine or vitamin A |
> **The most common real-world poisoning is not an exotic ingredient.** It is a plate of leftovers containing onion or garlic, given by someone being kind.
## Household non-foods worth knowing

- **Permethrin**, in dog flea treatments — severely toxic and a frequent cause of death
- **Paracetamol / acetaminophen** — cats lack the enzyme to process it; a single tablet can be fatal
- **Antifreeze (ethylene glycol)** — sweet-tasting, rapidly fatal, requires immediate treatment
- **Essential oils and diffusers**, especially tea tree, citrus, pine and eucalyptus
**Never give a cat human medication** unless your vet has prescribed that exact drug and dose.
## If you think your cat has eaten something

1. **Phone the vet or an animal poison line immediately.** Do not wait for symptoms.
2. **Do not induce vomiting** unless specifically instructed — it can cause more harm.
3. **Take the packaging** with you.
4. **Note the time and the estimated amount.**
5. If it is on the coat, **stop the cat grooming** — a buster collar or a towel wrap, then wash it off.
Many of these are far more treatable when caught early. Waiting for symptoms is what turns a treatable exposure into a fatal one.
## The short version

Onion and garlic in leftovers, lilies on the windowsill, and paracetamol in the drawer are the three that actually kill cats. Everything else on the list is worth knowing, and those three are worth acting on today.
*General guidance only. In a suspected poisoning, contact your vet or a pet poison helpline immediately.*

title: Human Foods Cats Can Safely Eat
excerpt: A short list, in small amounts, prepared plainly.
body: *Sharing is fine. The rules are: plain, small, and never more than a tenth of the day's calories.*

![A market display of fresh vegetables](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1553546895-531931aa1aa8?auto=format&fit=crop&w=1200&q=80)
*Cats are carnivores, so most of the safe list is meat. The plant entries are for fibre, not nutrition.*
## The three rules

1. **Plain.** No salt, oil, butter, onion, garlic, herbs or sauce. Seasoning is what makes most human food unsafe.
2. **Small.** Treats and extras stay under **10% of daily calories** — around 20 kcal for a 4 kg cat.
3. **One at a time.** Introduce a single new food and wait a couple of days, so a reaction has an obvious cause.
## Safe proteins

| Food | How to serve |
|---|---|
| **Cooked chicken** | Skinless, boneless, poached, no seasoning |
| **Cooked turkey** | Same. Avoid the skin and any stuffing |
| **Cooked beef or lamb** | Lean, plain, small pieces |
| **Cooked white fish** | Cod, haddock, plaice. Bones removed |
| **Tinned fish in spring water** | Drained. Occasional, not routine |
| **Cooked egg** | Scrambled or boiled, no butter or salt |
| **Cooked liver** | A very small piece. Excess causes vitamin A toxicity |
| **Plain cooked prawns** | Deveined, unseasoned |
Meat is the part of your dinner a cat is actually built for. Everything below is optional.
## Safe plant foods, in small amounts

- **Plain pumpkin purée** — 100% pumpkin, never pie filling. Useful fibre for hairballs and mild constipation
- **Cooked carrot** — soft, plain, tiny pieces
- **Cooked green beans, peas** — low calorie, some cats enjoy them
- **Cooked sweet potato or plain squash** — small amounts
- **Blueberries** — some cats like them, most ignore them
- **Watermelon and cantaloupe**, seedless and rindless — mostly water
- **Cooked plain rice or oats** — bland carriers, not nutrition
- **Cat grass or catnip** — genuinely enriching, and safer than chewing houseplants
> Cats have no dietary need for fruit or vegetables. These are safe rather than beneficial, with pumpkin's fibre the main real exception.
## Foods people wrongly think are fine
**Milk.** The cartoon saucer is bad advice. Most adult cats are lactose intolerant, and the result is diarrhoea. If you want the gesture, use a lactose-free cat milk, sparingly.
**Cheese.** Same lactose problem, plus fat and salt. A crumb as a pill wrapper is fine; a habit is not.
**Tuna as a staple.** Fine occasionally. Fed daily it is unbalanced, and cats develop a genuine fixation that makes them refuse balanced food.
**Raw egg white.** Contains avidin, which binds biotin, plus a salmonella risk. Cook it.
**Dog food.** Not toxic, but not supplemented for feline taurine, vitamin A or arachidonic acid. One stolen mouthful is nothing; regular feeding causes deficiency.
## The fast reference
**Yes, plain and small:** cooked chicken, turkey, beef, white fish, egg, plain pumpkin, cooked carrot, green beans, melon, a little tinned fish in water.
**No, ever:** onion, garlic, leek, chives, chocolate, coffee, alcohol, grapes, raisins, xylitol, raw dough, cooked bones, anything heavily salted.
## Making it useful

- **Use scraps as puzzle rewards** rather than bowl toppers, so food earns activity
- **Warm slightly** to lift the aroma, which is what drives feline appetite
- **Deduct from the main meal** on days you share
- **Feed away from the table**, or you are training a cat to beg for the rest of its life
## The short version
Plain cooked meat is the safe answer nearly every time. Vegetables are optional, dairy is a myth, and the seasoning on your plate is the real hazard.
*General guidance only. Introduce new foods slowly, and check with your vet for cats with kidney, urinary or digestive conditions.*

title: How to Switch Your Cat's Food Without a Hunger Strike
excerpt: Cats form food preferences early and defend them fiercely. Go slower than feels necessary.
body: *Dogs change food overnight. Cats treat a new texture as evidence of a trap.*

![A cat on a wooden table](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1616668983570-a971956d8928?auto=format&fit=crop&w=1200&q=80)
*Neophobia is normal. So is the standoff that follows a sudden switch.*
## Why cats resist

Kittens form preferences for texture, shape and aroma in their first months, and those preferences last. Cats are also **neophobic** — cautious of unfamiliar food — which in the wild protects against eating something harmful.

There is a second, sharper reason to go slowly. Cats develop **learned aversions**: if a food coincides with nausea, they can refuse that food permanently. Switch abruptly, upset the stomach, and you may lose the new diet forever.
## The ten-day method
Mix thoroughly rather than placing the foods side by side, or a picky cat will simply eat around the new one.
**For a fussy cat, stretch it to three or four weeks.** Move to the next stage only once the current one is being eaten cleanly. If the cat stalls, drop back one step and hold.
## When the cat refuses anyway

1. **Warm the food** slightly to body temperature. Aroma drives feline appetite more than taste.
2. **Use a flat, wide plate.** Deep bowls press on the whiskers, and some cats will not tolerate it.
3. **Add a topper** — a spoon of the cooking water from plain chicken, or a little juice from a tin of fish in spring water.
4. **Feed in a quiet spot**, away from the tray, the water and other pets.
5. **Remove uneaten wet food after 30 minutes** and offer fresh later, so the cat learns food is an event.
6. **Stop free feeding** during a transition. A cat grazing on old kibble has no reason to try anything new.

> **Never starve a cat into accepting food.** A cat that stops eating for even a couple of days risks **hepatic lipidosis**, a life-threatening liver failure. If a cat has not eaten in 24 hours, go back to the old food and call your vet.
## Texture is often the real obstacle
A cat refusing "the new food" is frequently refusing a new **format**. Pâté, chunks in gravy, chunks in jelly, mousse and shreds are entirely different experiences.
If a switch fails, try the same brand and flavour in another texture before concluding the cat dislikes it.
## Special cases
**Prescription diets.** These are worth extra patience, because the alternative is a cat with untreated disease. Ask your vet for samples of several textures, and take four weeks if needed.
**Dry to wet.** Often the hardest direction. Start by adding a teaspoon of wet beside the kibble rather than mixed in, and build from there.
**Multi-cat homes.** Transition everyone together, or feed separately. A cat that can eat its housemate's old food will.
**Kittens to adult food.** Around twelve months, over the same ten days. There is no rush.
## The short version
Ten days minimum, longer for a fussy cat, mixed rather than side by side. Warm it, use a flat dish, and never let a standoff run past 24 hours without calling your vet.
*General guidance only. A cat that refuses food for 24 hours needs veterinary advice, not persistence.*

title: Raw Feeding: An Honest Guide
excerpt: The claims, the real risks, and what to do if you decide to go ahead.
body: *Few subjects in cat ownership generate more heat. Here is what is actually established and what is not.*

![Raw steak in a cast iron pan](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1615937657715-bc7b4b7962c1?auto=format&fit=crop&w=1200&q=80)
*The argument for raw is evolutionary. The arguments against are microbiological and nutritional.*
## The case people make for it

Cats evolved eating whole small prey: raw muscle, organ, bone and viscera, high in protein and moisture, very low in carbohydrate. A well-formulated raw diet is genuinely closer to that than most kibble.
Owners commonly report better coat condition, smaller and less odorous stools, and good weight control. Those observations are real, though a well-chosen wet food often produces the same results.
## Where the evidence actually stands

**Nutritional completeness is the biggest issue.** Studies of home-prepared raw diets repeatedly find nutritional imbalances — commonly calcium and phosphorus wrong relative to each other, and inadequate taurine or vitamin A. Deficiencies take months to appear and some, such as taurine-linked retinal damage, are **permanent**.
