**Pathogen contamination is well documented.** *Salmonella*, *Campylobacter*, *Listeria* and *E. coli* are found in a substantial share of tested raw pet foods, including commercial products. Cats often carry these without symptoms and **shed them in faeces**, which is a household transmission route.
**Bones carry mechanical risk.** Raw bone is more flexible than cooked and less prone to splinter, but fractured teeth, obstruction and perforation still occur.
> Major veterinary bodies, including the American and British veterinary associations, advise against raw meat diets for pets, principally on public health grounds rather than nutrition.
## Who should not raw feed
This is the part that matters most, and it is about the humans as much as the cat.

- Households with **infants or young children**
- Anyone **pregnant**
- Anyone **elderly or immunocompromised** — chemotherapy, transplant medication, HIV, autoimmune treatment
- Cats with **inflammatory bowel disease, cancer or immune suppression**
- Cats with **kidney disease**, where phosphorus must be controlled precisely
In these situations the risk-benefit calculation clearly does not favour raw.
## If you decide to go ahead

**Use a complete commercial raw diet** formulated to AAFCO or FEDIAF standards, ideally **high-pressure processed** to reduce pathogens without cooking. Home-assembling from butcher's meat is where most of the documented harm comes from.
If you must prepare it yourself, work from a recipe written by a **board-certified veterinary nutritionist** for your specific cat. Generic internet ratios are not adequate.
### Handling, every time

1. Keep raw pet food **frozen** until use; thaw in the fridge, never on the counter
2. Use a **separate board, knife and bowl**, and never the ones used for human food
3. Disinfect every surface after contact — hot soapy water then a disinfectant
4. **Wash hands thoroughly** before and after
5. Discard uneaten food after **20 minutes**
6. Wash the cat's bowl after every meal
7. Be scrupulous with the litter tray, since shedding continues for weeks
## A middle path worth considering

Most of the benefits people seek from raw — high protein, high moisture, low carbohydrate, minimal processing — are available from a **good-quality wet food**, without the pathogen and formulation risks.
If the appeal is species-appropriate feeding rather than rawness itself, a high-protein, low-carbohydrate wet diet gets you most of the way there.
## The short version

Raw feeding can be done safely, but only with a complete commercial diet, disciplined hygiene, and no vulnerable people in the house. Home-mixed raw is where cats get hurt, and the damage is often invisible until it is permanent.
*General guidance only. Discuss any raw diet with your vet, particularly for kittens, seniors, or cats with existing disease.*

title: Feeding a Kitten Through the First Year
excerpt: Twelve months of growth on a stomach the size of a walnut.
body: *A kitten multiplies its birth weight many times over in a few months. Its stomach does not grow nearly as fast.*

![A kitten sitting on a wooden floor](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1615789591457-74a63395c990?auto=format&fit=crop&w=1200&q=80)
*Little and often is not a preference. It is a physical constraint.*
## Why kitten food is different

Growth needs roughly **two to three times** the energy per kilo of an adult cat, plus more protein, more calcium and phosphorus in the right ratio, and **DHA**, an omega-3 that supports brain and retinal development.
Adult food does not meet this. A kitten raised on it grows more slowly and can end up with skeletal problems.
Look for a label stating the food is complete for **growth** or **all life stages**.
## The schedule

| Age | Food | Meals per day |
|---|---|---|
| 0–4 weeks | Queen's milk, or kitten milk replacer | On demand, every 2–4 hours |
| 4–8 weeks | Weaning: kitten wet food, softened with water | 4–6 |
| 2–4 months | Kitten wet and dry | 4 |
| 4–6 months | Kitten wet and dry | 3 |
| 6–12 months | Kitten food, portions adjusted | 2–3 |
| From 12 months | Transition to adult over 10 days | 2 |
**Never give cow's milk.** Kittens lack the enzymes for it and it causes diarrhoea, which is dangerous at this size. Orphaned kittens need a proper kitten milk replacer.
> Large breeds such as Maine Coons keep growing well past a year. Ask your vet when to switch — for some, kitten food continues to 18 months.
## Weaning, week by week
Around four weeks, kittens start showing interest in solid food.

1. Mix kitten wet food with kitten milk replacer to a thin gruel
2. Offer it on a **flat saucer** — they will walk in it, and that is part of learning
3. Thicken gradually over two to three weeks
4. By seven or eight weeks most kittens eat solid food comfortably
5. Keep fresh water available from four weeks onward
## Getting the amount right
Follow the packet as a starting point, but judge by the kitten. It should be:

- **Rounded but not distended.** A bloated belly after every meal means portions are too large
- **Gaining steadily.** Weigh weekly — roughly 100 g a week in early months is a common pattern
- **Energetic between naps**, with a soft, glossy coat
**Free feeding dry food is more acceptable in kittens** than adults, because their energy needs are genuinely high. Move to measured meals by six months, or the habit outlives the need.
## Building a cat that is not fussy
The window for food preferences is early and it does not reopen.

- **Offer several textures** — pâté, chunks, gravy, jelly, dry
- **Offer several proteins** — chicken, fish, turkey, rabbit
- **Use different bowl types and locations**
- **Handle the food and the kitten calmly** so mealtimes are unremarkable
A kitten given only one food for twelve months becomes an adult that refuses everything else, which is a genuine problem the day a prescription diet is needed.
## Things to avoid

- **Cow's milk** — diarrhoea
- **Adult cat food** before twelve months — insufficient for growth
- **Dog food** — no taurine supplementation
- **Raw diets** — kittens have immature immune systems and the highest deficiency stakes
- **Free access to treats** — the 10% rule applies from the start
- **Bones of any kind**
## The short version
Complete kitten food, four small meals a day dropping to two by a year, weighed weekly, with as many textures and proteins as you can offer while the window is open.
*General guidance only. Orphaned or hand-reared kittens need veterinary guidance from the start.*

title: Why Cats Knead (and Why It Hurts)
excerpt: Making biscuits is a leftover from kittenhood that never switched off.
body: *Rhythmic paw-pushing on a lap, a blanket, or your stomach at three in the morning. Cats do it their whole lives, and the reason starts in the first week of theirs.*

![A relaxed tabby lying on a sofa](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1518791841217-8f162f1e1131?auto=format&fit=crop&w=1200&q=80)
*Kneading almost always happens in a settled, safe posture.*
## Where the behaviour comes from
Newborn kittens knead against their mother while nursing. The pressure stimulates milk flow, and the action is paired from the very beginning with warmth, safety and being fed.
That association is laid down before a kitten can see properly, and it never fully goes away. An adult cat kneading is running a comfort behaviour learned in its first days.
Kittens weaned early — orphans, or those separated before eight weeks — often knead more intensely as adults, and are the ones most likely to suckle fabric at the same time.
## The other three reasons
**Scent marking.** Cats have scent glands in the pads of their paws. Kneading deposits a personal chemical signature. Your lap is being claimed, quietly and repeatedly.
**Nest preparation.** Wild cats tread down grass and leaves before settling. Kneading a blanket into shape is the same instinct with no grass available.
**Sociability and mating.** Females often knead more around oestrus, and cats knead against each other during affiliative contact.
> Kneading is a **contentment signal**. A frightened or unwell cat does not knead. Take it as a compliment, however sharp.
## Why it hurts, and what to do
Claws extend during kneading, because the toes spread as part of the motion. The cat is not attacking you and does not understand that it hurts.
Things that work:

- **Keep a folded blanket or thick towel nearby** and slide it under the cat when kneading starts. This is by far the most effective fix
- **Trim the claws** regularly, taking only the clear tip well away from the pink quick
- **Wear something thick** on the lap in the evening if there is a routine to it
- **Gently redirect** by moving the cat to a cushion beside you
Things that do not work:

- **Pushing the cat off.** It reads as rejection and does nothing for the instinct
- **Punishment of any kind.** You would be punishing a contentment signal, which damages trust
- **Declawing.** An amputation of the last toe bone, banned in many countries, causing lasting pain and behavioural problems
## When kneading comes with suckling
Some cats suckle blanket, wool or an earlobe while kneading. It is common in early-weaned cats and in Siamese and other Oriental breeds.
It is usually harmless. Watch for two things:

- **Wool eating rather than sucking.** Swallowed fabric can cause intestinal obstruction, which is surgical
- **A sudden increase** in an adult cat that never did it, which can indicate stress or anxiety
Redirect toward a dedicated blanket the cat is allowed to have, and remove anything it might actually swallow.
## When to pay attention
Kneading itself is essentially never a medical sign. Consider a vet visit if you also notice:

- Kneading paired with restlessness, pacing or vocalising, which can indicate discomfort
- Repeated kneading of one specific spot on its own body
- A sudden stop in a cat that always kneaded, alongside hiding or reduced grooming — a common early sign that something hurts
## The short version
Your cat is running a nursing reflex, marking you as its own, and telling you it feels safe. Put a blanket down and keep the claws trimmed.

title: When a Cat Stops Using the Litter Tray
excerpt: It is never spite. It is medical, aversion, or stress, in that order.
body: *This is the leading behavioural reason cats are surrendered to shelters. It is also one of the most fixable.*

![A black and white cat resting](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1603104010974-de673b7c5674?auto=format&fit=crop&w=1200&q=80)
*A cat avoiding the tray is reporting a problem, not registering a protest.*
## Rule one: the vet comes first
**Always.** Before any behavioural theory, before buying a new tray, before anything.

Cystitis, crystals, bladder stones, urinary infection, kidney disease, diabetes, arthritis and constipation all cause tray avoidance. The mechanism is simple and cruel: the cat feels pain while in the tray, associates the pain with the place, and starts going elsewhere.
**A male cat straining with little output is an emergency.** A urethral blockage can be fatal within a day or two.
> Treating a medical problem as misbehaviour is how a treatable illness becomes a rehomed cat.
## Rule two: it is not spite

Cats do not conduct revenge campaigns. They do not understand that urinating on a bed is meaningful to you. Owners read intention into it because the locations feel personal, and they feel personal because they smell most strongly of you — which is exactly why an anxious cat chooses them.
**Punishment makes it worse in every case.** It adds stress to a stress behaviour and teaches the cat to hide, not to change.
## Marking versus toileting
These look different and mean different things.

| | Spraying / marking | Inappropriate toileting |
|---|---|---|
| Posture | Standing, tail quivering, backed up to a vertical surface | Squatting normally |
| Surface | Walls, doors, furniture edges, bags | Floors, beds, carpets, baths |
| Volume | Small | A full bladder |
| Meaning | Territorial or social stress | Something is wrong with the tray or the cat |
Marking is communication. It rises with a new pet, a new baby, building work, a house move, or an unfamiliar cat visible through a window.
## The tray audit
Once your vet has cleared the cat, work through the setup honestly.

- **Number.** One tray per cat, **plus one spare**. Two cats need three.
- **Location.** Spread out, on different floors. Two trays side by side count as one.
- **Size.** About **1.5 times the cat's body length**. Most commercial trays are too small.
- **Cover.** Remove it. Hoods trap odour and remove escape routes, and many cats dislike them.
- **Litter.** Unscented, fine-grained and clumping wins most preference tests. Cats generally dislike scented litter, and it is sold to owners rather than cats.
- **Depth.** About 5 cm.
- **Cleaning.** Scoop daily, full change and wash weekly. Avoid strongly scented cleaners, and never use anything containing ammonia — it smells like urine.
- **Access.** For older cats, a low entry. Stepping over a high side is a real barrier for stiff joints.
- **Privacy.** Away from the washing machine, the food, the water, and the dog.
## Cleaning what has already happened
You must remove the scent, not mask it. A cat returns to a spot it can still smell.

1. Blot, do not rub
2. Use an **enzymatic cleaner** made for pet urine, which digests the compounds rather than covering them
3. **Never use ammonia-based cleaners** — they smell like urine and invite a repeat
4. Soak the area properly and let it dry slowly; a quick wipe treats the surface only
5. While it heals, make the spot unattractive: foil, a plastic mat, or move a food bowl there
## Reducing the stress underneath

- Add **vertical space** — shelves, cat trees, windowsills
- Provide **hiding places** at floor level
- Keep resources **spread out** in multi-cat homes: food, water, trays, beds
- Block the view of outdoor cats with window film if that is the trigger
- Consider a **synthetic feline pheromone diffuser**
- Keep routines predictable
## The short version
Vet first, always. Then more trays, bigger and uncovered, unscented clumping litter, scooped daily, spread around the house. Punishment has no place anywhere in this process.
*General guidance only. Sudden tray avoidance needs veterinary examination, and straining with little output is an emergency.*

title: How to Stop a Cat Scratching the Furniture
excerpt: You cannot stop the scratching. You can move it.
body: *Scratching is not a bad habit. It is a physical need, a communication system and a stretch, all at once.*

![A Siamese cat scratching a chair leg](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1759165440303-40ef25cc6053?auto=format&fit=crop&w=1200&q=80)
*The sofa is not being attacked. It is being used correctly, from the cat's point of view.*
## What scratching actually does
Four jobs at the same time:

1. **Claw maintenance.** It strips the worn outer sheath from the front claws, exposing the sharp layer underneath.
2. **Scent marking.** Glands between the toes leave a chemical signal. Scratching is a message board.
3. **Visual marking.** The shredded marks themselves are a signal to other cats.
4. **Stretching.** A full-body stretch of the spine, shoulders and forelimbs.

Because it is partly communication, **cats scratch in socially important places** — near doorways, beside sleeping spots, and along the routes they use most. The sofa in the middle of the living room is not a coincidence.
> You cannot train a cat out of scratching, any more than you can train it out of stretching. The goal is redirection, never suppression.
## Why your post is being ignored
Most rejected scratching posts fail on one of four counts.
**Too short.** A cat wants a **full stretch** — for most adults that means at least 80 cm of usable height. Many sold posts are half that.
**Too wobbly.** A post that rocks under weight is unusable. It must be heavy-based or wall-mounted.
**Wrong material.** Sisal rope and sisal fabric are the most reliably preferred. Carpet is a poor choice, because it teaches the cat that carpet is for scratching.
**Wrong place.** A post exiled to the spare room serves no marking purpose. It has to go where the cat already scratches.
## The method that works

1. **Put a post directly next to the damaged furniture.** Not across the room. Touching it.
2. **Match the orientation.** A cat that scratches the carpet wants a horizontal pad; one that scratches chair legs wants a vertical post.
3. **Make the furniture unpleasant.** Double-sided tape, aluminium foil or a plastic mat over the spot. Cats dislike the texture on their pads.
4. **Make the post attractive.** Rub catnip in, dangle a toy from it, feed treats at its base.
5. **Reward every use.** Praise or a treat the moment they use it.
6. **Once it is established**, move the post a few centimetres a day toward where you want it. Slowly.
7. **Provide several posts.** One per major room, plus one near where the cat sleeps — cats scratch immediately on waking.
## Claw trimming
Trimming reduces damage substantially, and it is easy once the cat accepts it.

- Trim only the **clear tip**, staying well back from the pink quick
- Front claws every two to three weeks
- Do one or two claws per session if that is all the cat allows
- Use proper cat clippers, not scissors
**Vinyl claw caps** are a legitimate option for problem cases. They glue over the claw, last four to six weeks, and are harmless.
## What never to do

**Never declaw.** It is not a nail trim. It amputates the last bone of each toe, comparable to removing a human finger at the last joint. It is banned in the UK, much of Europe and many other jurisdictions, and it is associated with chronic pain, litter tray avoidance and increased biting.
**Never punish.** Shouting, spraying water or smacking teaches the cat to fear you, not to stop scratching. It will scratch when you leave the room.
## The short version
Buy a tall, rigid, sisal post. Put it right next to the furniture that is being scratched, make the furniture unpleasant, and reward the post. That combination solves most cases within a fortnight.

title: Play Is a Hunt, and Most Owners Cut It Short
excerpt: A cat needs to finish the sequence: stalk, chase, catch, kill, eat.
body: *A laser pointer gives a cat the chase and denies it the catch. That is why it can leave a cat more wound up than before.*

![An orange cat playing with a toy](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1691351943492-cfee023e9cbf?auto=format&fit=crop&w=1200&q=80)
*Play is not entertainment. It is a behavioural need with a defined shape.*
## The predatory sequence
Wild cats hunt in a fixed pattern, and each stage is separately rewarding:

1. **Stare** — locate the prey
2. **Stalk** — approach low and slow
3. **Pounce** — the explosive rush
4. **Catch** — physical contact, grabbing with the front paws
5. **Kill bite** — the back-leg rabbit kick and the bite
6. **Eat** — consumption

Domestic cats keep the whole sequence even when fed. It runs on its own schedule, and a cat that never gets to complete it accumulates frustration that surfaces as ankle ambushes, night zoomies, overgrooming and redirected aggression.
> The most common play mistake is providing stage three and stopping. The cat needs the catch.
## The laser pointer problem

A laser is excellent at triggering stalk, chase and pounce. It is physically impossible to catch. Some cats handle it fine; others develop visible frustration, and a minority become fixated on lights and reflections.
If you use one, **always finish by landing the dot on a physical toy or a few treats**, and let the cat catch that. It closes the sequence.
## How to play properly
**Use a wand toy.** It puts distance between your hands and the claws, and it lets you move the toy like prey rather than like a hand.
**Move it like an animal**, which means *away* and *hiding*. Prey does not fly at a cat's face. Drag it around a corner, let it disappear behind a chair, pause completely, then twitch.
**Use pauses.** A stationary toy that suddenly moves triggers the pounce. Constant motion becomes background.
**Let the cat win.** Regularly. A cat that never catches anything stops trying.
**Finish with a catch and then food.** Play, catch, then a meal or a few treats. This mirrors the natural hunt-eat cycle and is the single best way to settle a cat before the night.
### The routine

- **Two sessions a day**, five to fifteen minutes each
- Best times: **early morning and evening**, when cats are naturally most active
- Stop while the cat is still interested, not once it is exhausted
- **Rotate toys** weekly — cats habituate fast, and a stored toy becomes new again
## Toys that earn their place

| Type | Why it works |
|---|---|
| Wand toys with feathers or fabric | Full sequence, hands protected |
| Small realistic mice | Right size and weight for carrying and kicking |
| Kicker toys | Made for the back-leg kick stage |
| Puzzle feeders and food balls | Add the hunting-for-food element |
| Crinkle balls and paper bags | Cheap, and sound matters as much as sight |
| Cardboard boxes | Ambush points, which are part of hunting |
**Avoid** string, tinsel, hair ties and rubber bands left out unsupervised. Linear foreign bodies are a serious surgical emergency in cats.
## Never play with hands
Wrestling with fingers teaches a kitten that hands are prey. It is charming at ten weeks and a real problem at three years, and it is very hard to undo.
If a cat grabs your hand, **go completely still**. Movement triggers more biting. Wait for release, then end the session without drama.
## The short version
Two short sessions a day with a wand toy, moved like fleeing prey, with real catches allowed and a meal at the end. That single routine resolves a surprising share of feline behaviour problems.

title: Introducing a Second Cat, Properly
excerpt: Take three weeks. Rushing it can create a conflict that lasts for years.
body: *Most failed cat introductions fail in the first hour, because the cats were allowed to meet in it.*

![Two cats lying together](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1532386236358-a33d8a9434e3?auto=format&fit=crop&w=1200&q=80)
*This is the destination. It is reached slowly.*
## Start from the right assumption

Cats are **facultatively social**. They can live in groups, and free-living colonies form readily — but those are usually related females who grew up together, in a territory with enough resources for everyone.
Two unrelated adults in a flat is not that situation. It can work well, and it depends on doing the introduction properly and on getting the resources right afterwards.
> A first meeting that goes badly can set a pattern that takes months to undo. Almost all of the work is in preventing that first bad experience.
## Week one: complete separation
The new cat lives in **one closed room** with its own litter tray, food, water, bed, scratching post and toys.
They do not see each other. They hear and smell each other under the door, which is the point.

- Let the new cat settle and explore its room
- Spend time in there so it associates you with safety
- **Scent swap** daily: rub a soft cloth on one cat's cheeks and leave it where the other sleeps
- Swap bedding between the two spaces
- Once the new cat is confident, **swap the cats over** for an hour so each explores the other's territory without contact
Do not move on until both cats are eating normally and neither is hissing at the door.
## Week two: feed on either side of the door
Place both food bowls near the closed door, far enough apart that both eat calmly. Over several days, move them closer.
This builds the association you want: *the other cat's smell means good things happen.*
If either cat stops eating, growls or backs off, **move the bowls further apart** and slow down. That is not failure, it is the process working.
## Week three: visual contact, controlled
Introduce sight without the possibility of contact. A tall baby gate, a door cracked and wedged a few centimetres, or a screen.

- Keep sessions **short** — a few minutes at first
- Feed or play on both sides during the sessions
- **End before anything goes wrong**, while both are still calm
- Repeat many times a day, building duration
Staring, flattened ears or a puffed tail means you have gone too fast. Close it and go back a stage.
## Week four: supervised freedom
Open the door and let them share the space, with you present.

- Keep sessions short and positive, and be boring yourself
- Have a **towel or cushion** ready to interrupt a fight — **never your hands**
- Do not pick either cat up mid-conflict
- Some hissing and swatting is normal negotiation. Screaming, chasing and sustained flat-out fighting is not
- Build up gradually before leaving them unsupervised
## Resources are what keep the peace
Most long-term conflict is competition, not personality. The rule is **one per cat plus one**, spread out.

| Resource | For two cats |
|---|---|
| Litter trays | 3, in different rooms |
| Food stations | 2+, apart and out of sight of each other |
| Water bowls | 2+, away from the food |
| Beds and hiding spots | Several, at different heights |
| Scratching posts | 2+ |
**Vertical space matters more than floor space.** Shelves, cat trees and windowsills let cats share a room while keeping distance, and let a lower-ranking cat pass without confrontation.
## Signs it is going wrong

- One cat blocking access to the tray, food or a doorway
- A cat that stops eating, hides constantly, or urinates outside the tray
- Fights that draw blood or produce screaming
- One cat confined to a single room by the other
Any of these means going back several stages, and asking your vet about a referral to a behaviourist. Cat conflict is often subtle — much of it is silent blocking rather than fighting.
## The short version
Four weeks: separation, then smell, then food through a door, then sight, then supervised contact. Add one more of everything than you have cats, and put half of it up high.

title: Why Do Cats Purr? It Is Not Only Happiness
excerpt: Cats purr when content, when frightened, when injured, and while dying.
body: *The most misread sound in the animal kingdom.*

![A happy cat looking up](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1543852786-1cf6624b9987?auto=format&fit=crop&w=1200&q=80)
*Content, certainly. But contentment is only one of the reasons.*
## How the sound is made
Purring comes from the **laryngeal muscles**, which rapidly open and close the glottis, interrupting airflow. That produces the characteristic vibration, typically between about **25 and 150 Hz**.
The distinctive feature is that it runs on **both the in-breath and the out-breath**, which is why it sounds continuous. Almost no other vocalisation does this.
Kittens begin purring at only a few days old, while nursing, and their mother purrs back. It is one of the earliest forms of communication a cat has.
## Purring is a request, not a report
The most useful reframing: purring generally means **"keep doing this"** or **"I need something"** rather than "I am happy."
Cats purr:

- While being stroked, in contentment
- While nursing, and while being nursed
- **At the vet**, frightened, as self-soothing
- **When injured**, sometimes severely
- **When ill or dying**, which distresses owners who read it as comfort
- **When hungry**, in a specific pattern described below
> Never use purring to rule out pain. A purring cat at the vet is frequently a stressed cat trying to calm itself.
## The solicitation purr
Researchers have identified a distinct purr that cats use when they want feeding. Embedded in the low rumble is a **higher-frequency cry**, in a range close to that of a human infant's cry.
Humans rate this purr as more urgent and harder to ignore. Cats living with people develop it; it is far less common in colony cats. Your cat may well have learned it specifically on you.
## The healing hypothesis

Purring frequencies sit in a range that laboratory work has associated with **promoting bone density and tissue repair**. It has been proposed that purring is partly a self-repair mechanism, which would explain why cats purr while injured and while resting.
It is a plausible and attractive idea, and it is not settled science. Treat it as an interesting hypothesis rather than an established fact.
## Which cats purr
Purring belongs to the smaller cats: domestic cats, cheetahs, bobcats, lynx.

The big roaring cats — lions, tigers, leopards, jaguars — have a differently structured hyoid apparatus. They roar, and they cannot purr continuously. The trade-off appears to be roughly one or the other.
## Reading it in context
Purring alone tells you very little. Combine it with posture:

| Purr plus… | Reading |
|---|---|
| Loose body, slow blink, kneading | Genuine contentment |
| Weaving at your legs near the kitchen | Solicitation — hunger |
| Tense body, flattened ears, hiding | Stress or fear |
| Hunched posture, reduced grooming, off food | **Possible pain — see a vet** |
| Rapid breathing, open mouth | **Urgent — see a vet** |
## The short version
Purring means a cat wants the current situation to continue or to change. It is a signal of need, not of joy, and it can accompany serious illness. Read the body, not the sound.
*General guidance only. A purring cat that is hiding, hunched or not eating needs veterinary attention.*

title: Night Zoomies and the Cat Sleep Cycle
excerpt: Cats are not nocturnal. They are crepuscular, which is why 5am is the problem.
body: *Your cat is not broken. It is running on dawn-and-dusk timing that predates your alarm clock by a few million years.*

![A white cat asleep under a duvet](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1541781774459-bb2af2f05b55?auto=format&fit=crop&w=1200&q=80)
*Cats sleep a great deal, in short blocks, at times that suit them.*
## Crepuscular, not nocturnal
Cats are most active at **dawn and dusk**. Their prey — small rodents and birds — is most active then, and the low light suits feline eyes, which work with roughly a sixth of the light we need.
This is why the 4am sprint down the hallway happens. It is not misbehaviour or insomnia. It is a hunting window opening on schedule.
Cats sleep around **12 to 16 hours a day**, in many short bouts rather than one long block, most of it light dozing with the ears still tracking.
## Why the zoomies happen
The proper term is **frenetic random activity period**. Common triggers:

- **Accumulated energy** in a cat that has not hunted, played or worked for food all day
- **The crepuscular window** arriving on time
- **After a litter tray visit**, oddly common and probably a relief-and-release response
- **After a nap**, as a full-body wake-up
- **Boredom**, in an under-stimulated indoor cat
In kittens and young adults it is normal and healthy. What matters is whether the household can live with the timing.
## Shifting the schedule
You cannot make a cat diurnal. You can move its main activity window earlier, and the mechanism is the natural **hunt, catch, eat, groom, sleep** cycle.

1. **Play hard in the evening**, ideally 20–30 minutes before your bedtime. Use a wand toy and let the cat make real catches.
2. **Feed the largest meal immediately after that play.** Completing the hunt-eat sequence is what triggers the grooming-and-sleeping phase.
3. **Add a second play session in the morning**, so daytime energy has somewhere to go.
4. **Use puzzle feeders during the day** so food takes effort rather than seconds.
5. **Consider a timed feeder** set for early morning. This is the single most effective fix for the 5am wake-up, because it breaks the link between *you waking* and *food arriving*.
## The mistake almost everyone makes

**Do not get up and feed a cat that wakes you.** Not once. A cat needs very few repetitions to learn that yowling at 5am produces breakfast, and intermittent reward — feeding sometimes — creates the most persistent behaviour of all.
The same applies to shouting or getting up to shut a door. Any response is a response.
Expect an **extinction burst**: when you stop responding, the behaviour gets worse for several days before it fades. Give it two weeks of consistency.
If the noise is unbearable in the meantime, shut the bedroom door and provide entertainment elsewhere, rather than intervening.
## Enrichment while you sleep

- A **puzzle feeder** left loaded overnight
- A **window perch**, which gives hours of watching
- **Rotate toys** so something is always novel
- A **cat tree** for climbing without a launch pad on your bed
## When night activity is medical
A sudden change in an adult or older cat deserves attention, not training. Consider a vet visit for:

- **New, loud night-time yowling in an older cat** — often hyperthyroidism, hypertension or feline cognitive dysfunction
- **Restlessness with weight loss and increased appetite** — classic hyperthyroidism
- **Disorientation, staring at walls, forgetting the tray** — cognitive decline
- **Pacing that looks uncomfortable rather than playful** — pain
> Zoomies in a two-year-old are normal. New night-time yowling in a fourteen-year-old is a symptom.
## The short version
Play hard, then feed, right before bed. Use a timed feeder for the early morning. Never respond to a 5am demand, and expect it to worsen before it stops.
*General guidance only. Sudden night-time vocalisation in an older cat needs veterinary assessment.*

title: Reading a Cat's Ears and Eyes
excerpt: Thirty-two muscles per ear, and pupils that report arousal as well as light.
body: *The tail carries the volume. The ears and eyes carry the detail.*

![A tabby cat against a blue sky](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1574158622682-e40e69881006?auto=format&fit=crop&w=1200&q=80)
*Ears forward, eyes soft, whiskers loose: a comfortable cat.*
## The ears

Each ear is controlled by around **32 muscles** and rotates independently through roughly 180 degrees. They are directional microphones, and they are also the fastest-moving part of a cat's emotional display.

| Ear position | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Forward, upright | Alert, interested, relaxed |
| Swivelling independently | Tracking a sound — not necessarily emotional |
| Slightly back, relaxed | Content, often while being stroked |
| Rotated back, upright | Irritated or uneasy — **a warning** |
| Flat sideways, "aeroplane ears" | Frightened or defensive; may strike |
| Flat back against the head | Very frightened or about to attack |

The critical one to learn is **aeroplane ears** — flattened out to the sides rather than backwards. It signals fear plus high arousal, and it is the position that most reliably precedes a defensive bite or swipe.
## The eyes
### Pupils
Pupils respond to light, so **read them against the room's brightness**. A change with no change in light is the meaningful one.

- **Narrow vertical slits in bright light** — normal
- **Slits in dim light** — possible tension, focus or irritation
- **Wide and round in dim light** — normal
- **Wide and round in bright light** — fear, excitement or high arousal
- **Suddenly dilating during petting** — stop stroking now
Dilation reflects arousal without telling you the flavour of it. A cat about to pounce on a toy and a cat about to flee both have wide pupils. The rest of the body distinguishes them.
### Eyelids

- **Soft, half-closed eyes** — relaxed and trusting
- **Wide open, unblinking stare** — threat or intense focus. Between cats, a hard stare is a challenge
- **Squinting when not sleepy** — often **pain**, especially with a tight muzzle
- **Third eyelid visible** across the inner corner — usually illness. See a vet
## The slow blink
Narrowing the eyes and blinking slowly is a genuine affiliative signal, and it is one of the few pieces of cat communication that has been experimentally tested.

Researchers at the Universities of Sussex and Portsmouth found that when humans slow-blinked at cats, the cats were **more likely to slow-blink back**, and more likely to approach the person's outstretched hand — including with strangers.
How to do it:

1. Relax your face and avoid staring directly
2. Narrow your eyes slowly, then close them for about a second
3. Open slowly and look slightly away
Direct, unbroken eye contact does the opposite. This is why cats in a room full of people so often approach the person ignoring them.
## Putting it together

| Ears | Eyes | Reading |
|---|---|---|
| Forward | Soft, half-closed | Relaxed, approachable |
| Forward | Wide, fixed on a target | Hunting focus |
| Rotated back | Pupils widening | Irritation building — stop |
| Flat sideways | Wide and round | Frightened, may strike |
| Slightly back | Squinting, tight muzzle | **Possible pain** |
> One signal alone is a guess. Ears plus eyes plus tail is a reading.
## The short version
Watch the ears for the first flicker of irritation and the eyes for arousal and pain. Aeroplane ears mean stop; a slow blink means you are welcome.
*General guidance only. Squinting, a visible third eyelid or sudden changes in the eyes need veterinary attention.*

title: How to Make an Indoor Cat Genuinely Happy
excerpt: Indoor cats live longer. Whether they live better depends entirely on the room.
body: *Keeping a cat indoors adds years to its life and removes almost everything it evolved to do. The second part is fixable.*

![A cat playing on a cat tree in a living room](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1636543459630-8975a3548121?auto=format&fit=crop&w=1200&q=80)
*A well-designed room does most of the work.*
## What a cat actually needs

Not toys. Behaviours. A cat needs opportunities to **hunt, climb, scratch, hide, observe and choose**. Boredom in cats does not look like sulking; it looks like overgrooming, aggression, obesity, night yowling and litter tray problems.
The single biggest change most homes can make is not another toy. It is **going vertical**.
## Vertical space comes first
Cats are semi-arboreal. Height means safety, a better view, and the ability to avoid another cat without confrontation. A room with floor space only is, from a cat's point of view, a small room.

- A **cat tree** tall enough to see over the furniture
- **Wall shelves** arranged as a climbing route
- **Cleared windowsills** — the single most-used spot in most homes
- A **safe perch in every main room**
- **Escape routes** so a cat is never cornered
In multi-cat homes, vertical space reduces conflict more reliably than anything else.
## Make food into work
A bowl of kibble delivers a day's calories in ninety seconds. In the wild, that would have been ten to twenty separate hunts.

- **Puzzle feeders** and food balls
- **Snuffle mats** for wet food or treats
- **Scatter feeding** — throw the daily ration around the room
- **Hide small portions** in different places so the cat forages
- **Lick mats** for wet food, which are slow and calming
This is enrichment and weight control at the same time, and it costs nothing.
## Play with intent
Two sessions a day, five to fifteen minutes, morning and evening when cats are naturally most active.

Use a **wand toy** and move it like fleeing prey — away from the cat, behind furniture, with pauses. **Let the cat make real catches**, and finish with a meal. The hunt-catch-eat sequence is what produces a settled cat afterwards.
**Rotate toys weekly.** Cats habituate quickly; a toy put away for a fortnight comes back new.
## A window on the world
The window is the indoor cat's television, and it is close to free.

- A **perch or shelf** at the sill
- A **bird feeder** placed outside a favourite window
- **Cat grass** in a pot, which is safe to chew, unlike most houseplants
If watching outdoor cats causes stress rather than interest — staring, spraying, tension — apply frosted film to the lower half of the glass instead.
## Scratching, resting and hiding

- **Scratching posts** in the rooms the cat uses, tall enough for a full stretch, sisal rather than carpet
- **Beds at several heights and temperatures**, so the cat can choose
- **Hiding places at floor level** — a covered bed, a cardboard box, space under a chair
A cat with nowhere to hide is a cat with no way to self-regulate. Boxes are not a joke; they measurably reduce stress in shelter studies.
## Going outside, safely

- **Catio or secure balcony** — outdoor air with no traffic or predators
- **Cat-proof garden fencing**
- **Harness and lead**, which suits some cats and not others. Introduce indoors over weeks
- **A stroller**, genuinely useful for elderly or disabled cats
## Should you get a second cat?

Sometimes it helps and sometimes it makes things much worse. A second cat is not a substitute for owner interaction, and a badly matched pair creates chronic stress that shows up as spraying and illness.
Consider it if your cat is young, sociable and clearly under-stimulated. Be cautious with an older cat that has lived alone for years. Either way, introduce over **four weeks**.
## A weekly checklist

- [ ] Two play sessions a day, most days
- [ ] Food delivered through at least one puzzle or scatter feed
- [ ] Toys rotated
- [ ] Every main room has a perch and a hiding spot
- [ ] Scratching posts where the cat actually is
- [ ] A clear window view
- [ ] Litter trays clean and spread out
## The short version
Go vertical, make food into work, play twice a day with real catches, and give the cat a window and somewhere to hide. Indoor life is safe by default and good only by design.
